(p-444) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat Yunus, peace be upon him.

This surah is Meccan. Muqatil said: except for two verses, namely His saying, may He be blessed and exalted: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ [Yunus: 94], which was revealed in Medina. Al-Kalbi said: it is Meccan except for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it and among them are those who do not believe in it﴾ [Yunus: 40], which was revealed concerning the Jews in Medina. A group said: about forty verses at its beginning were revealed in Mecca, and the rest in Medina.

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾ ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them: "Warn the people, and give good tidings to those who believe that they have a sure standing (qadam sidq) with their Lord"? The disbelievers said: "Indeed, this is clearly a magician."﴾

The disagreement over the openings of the surahs has already been mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, and all those statements apply here. At this place there is a view specific to it. Ibn 'Abbas, Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Sha'bi said: "Ra" and "Ha Mim" and "Nun" are "al-Rahman," the word being cut short in the openings of these surahs. There is disagreement from Nafi' concerning the imalah (vowel-inclination) of the ra', and the analogical rule is that it should not be inclined. Likewise the reciters differed (p-445). The reason for those who incline the ra' is to indicate by this that it is a name of the letter, and not a letter in itself; the letter is only "ra."

As for His saying, "Tilka": it was said to mean "hadhihi" (this), and it may be that the meaning connects with "tilka" without our needing to supply another word in its place. The consideration of this word is built only upon the disagreement about the openings of the surahs, so reflect on it. As for "al-Kitab," Mujahid and Qatadah said: it refers to the Torah and the Gospel. Mujahid and others also said: it refers to the Qur'an, and this is the more evident. As for "al-Hakim," it is a form (fa'il) in the sense of muhkam (perfected), as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿This is what is ready with me (ladayya 'atid)﴾ [Qaf: 23], meaning prepared and readied. It is also possible that "hakim" means "possessing wisdom" (dhu hikmah), so it is in the sense of a relative adjective (nasab). al-Tabari said: "It is like alim in the sense of mu'lim (painful)." Then he said: it is He who perfected it and made it clear.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He mentioned two statements as though they were one.

As for His saying, ﴿Is it a wonder for the people﴾, the verse... Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, and others said: this verse was revealed because the Quraysh considered it unlikely that Allah would send a messenger from among mankind. al-Zajjaj said: they only wondered at his report that they would be raised from the graves, since warning and good tidings include that. Their talk about this increased, until some of them said: "Did Allah not find anyone to send except the orphan of Abu Talib?" and similar sayings which I have abridged because of their fame. Then the verse was revealed. His saying: "Akana" (is it) is an affirmation (taqrir), and the intended "people" are those who made this statement. "'Ajaban" is the predicate of "kana," and its subject is "an awhayna" (that We revealed). In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads "Akana lil-nasi 'ajabun," and the predicate was placed in His saying, glorified is He, "an awhayna." The first is more correct, because the subject is definite and the predicate is indefinite, and this reversal is not valid and occurs only as an anomaly; from it is the verse of Hassan:

"... its mixture is honey and water."

The word "'ajab" here does not mean only wonder, but its meaning is: their denial and amazement reached the point of denial? And a group read "ila rajulin" with a sukun on the jim. Then He explained the revelation and divided it into warning to the disbelievers and good tidings to the believers. "Qadam" here means: what one has sent forward. There is disagreement about what is meant by it here. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and Ibn Zayd said: it is righteous deeds of worship. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ). Zayd ibn Aslam and others said: it is the calamity of Muhammad (ﷺ) through his death. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, also said, and others: it is the happiness preordained for them in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), and this is the most fitting of the statements for the verse. From this word is the verse of Hassan:

"For us is the highest qadam toward you, and behind us ... follows our first in obedience to Allah."

(p-447) And the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"For you is a qadam that people do not deny, with lofty lineage it overflowed the sea."

From this word is also the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) describing Hell: "Until the Compeller places His foot (qadam) in it, and it says: Qat, qat," meaning what He has sent forward to it of His creation. This is according to the view that "al-Jabbar" is a name of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted. Whoever makes it a generic noun, as if he meant the tyrants among the children of Adam, then "qadam" on this interpretation is the limb. As for "sidq" in this verse, it means goodness, as you say: "a man of sidq" and "a man of su'" (evil). His saying, glorified is He: ﴿The disbelievers said﴾ may be an explanation of His saying: "Is it a wonder that We revealed to a man?" — the disbelievers said about it such and such? al-Tabari held that the speech contains an omission that the apparent meaning indicates, its estimated sense being: when he warned and gave good tidings, the disbelievers said such and such. The majority of readers, and it is the reading of Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir, read: "Inna hadha lasihrun mubin" (this is indeed clear magic). Masruq ibn al-Ajda', Ibn Jubayr, and the rest of the seven, and Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Razin, Mujahid, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, al-A'mash, Isa ibn Umar with a variant, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ibn Kathir with a variant from him read: "Inna hadha lasahirun" (this is indeed a magician), and the meaning is close. In the codex of Ubayy: "Qala al-kafirun ma hadha illa sihrun mubin" (the disbelievers said: this is nothing but clear magic). Their saying about the warning and good tidings being magic was only because he separated their unity by it and came between a person and his close relative, so it resembled what the magician does, and they thought it belonged to that category.

[p-449] Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne, arranging the affair. There is no intercessor except after His permission. That is Allah, your Lord, so worship Him. Will you not remember?﴾ ﴿To Him is your return, all of you. The promise of Allah is true. Indeed, He originates the creation, then repeats it, that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice. But those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾

This is the beginning of a call to the worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and an informing about His attributes. The address by them is to all people. The statement "He created the heavens and the earth" follows what is established: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created the earth, then turned to the heaven while it was smoke, so He created it, and afterwards He spread out the earth. As for His saying "in six days," it has been said that these are days of the Hereafter. But the majority, and this is the correct view, said: rather, they are days of this world.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is by way of estimation, because the sun and its movement had not yet come into being at that time. The statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) about Allah's creation of the creatures, "Allah began on Sunday such-and-such, and on such-and-such day..." is only to be understood as our estimating that time and reckoning back to it the measure of the day and night from the moment the sequence of day and night began. The well-known view is that Allah began the creation on Sunday, and in some hadiths in the Book of Muslim, and in al-Dala'il (of al-Bayhaqi), it occurred that the beginning was on Saturday. Some people mentioned that the wisdom in Allah's creating these things, may He be blessed and exalted, over a limited and extended period, while He had the power to say "Be" and it is, is that He might teach His servants deliberation and gradualness in affairs.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is among the matters whose reason cannot be reached. On this view, the embryos in the wombs and the creation of fruits and other things are the same, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made for everything a measure, and He knows best the wisdom in that.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾, the discussion of it has already passed at ﴿Al-Mṣ﴾ [al-A'raf: 1]. As for His saying ﴿arranging the affair﴾, it is valid that by "al-amr" He means the generic noun of affairs, and it is possible that He means the affair which is the verbal noun of "amara, ya'muru, amran" (he commanded). His arranging it, there is no god but Him, is only its execution, because He has encompassed everything in knowledge. Mujahid said: ﴿arranging the affair﴾ means: He decrees it alone.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿there is no intercessor except after His permission﴾, it is a refutation of the Arabs in their belief that the idols would intercede for them. As for His saying ﴿That﴾, it is a reference to Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, meaning: this One whose attributes are these, so worship Him. Then He confirmed them upon these signs and lessons, saying ﴿Will you not remember?﴾, meaning: so that remembrance may be a cause of guidance.

The summary of the discussion of His saying, glorified is He, ﴿then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾, is that it means He established Himself by His dominance and overpowering; or "istawa" may mean "istawla" (to take possession), if the word is correct in the language. It has been said regarding the verse of the poet:

"Bishr has taken possession of Iraq, without sword or spilled blood."

that it is a fabricated line. Or it may be that He did an act upon the Throne and called it "istawa." The full discussion has already passed.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾, the verse is a report of the resurrection from the graves, and it is among the matters that reason permits and that the Law has established as occurring. His saying "jami'an" (all of you) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "marji'ukum" (your return). "Wa'da Allah" (the promise of Allah) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and likewise His saying "ḥaqqan" (true). Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: "ḥaqqan" is an adjective. Al-Jumhur read "innahu" with a kasra on the alif, as a resumption of a new sentence. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', al-A'mash, Sahl ibn Shu'ayb, and Abdullah read "annahu" with a fatha on the alif; its position is accusative, according to the estimate "uḥiqqu annahu" (I affirm that he...). Al-Farra' said its position is nominative, according to the estimate "yaḥiqqu annahu" (it is true that he...).

[p-450] The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In my view it is permissible that "annahu" be a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿the promise of Allah﴾. Abu al-Fath said: if you wish, you may estimate: "because He originates the creation," meaning: whoever has this power is free of breaking the promise. And if you wish, you may estimate it as: "Allah promised truly that..." and the verbal noun "wa'd" (promise) does not govern it, because it has been qualified, and that indicates its completion and cuts off its governing. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "ḥaqqun" with a nominative, so it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "annahu." His saying ﴿He originates the creation﴾ means the first creation, while the repetition (i'āda) is the resurrection from the graves. Talha read "yubdi'u al-khalq" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the dāl. His saying "li-yajziya" (that He may reward) is the lam of purpose (lām kay), and the meaning is that the repetition is only so that the recompense falls upon the deeds. His saying "bil-qist" means with justice, in their being shown mercy and in the goodness of their reward. His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved﴾ is a new beginning. Al-ḥamīm (scalding water) is what is heated and made very hot; it is a form (fa'īl) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl), and from it come "al-ḥamām" (bath/heat) and "al-ḥummah" (fever). From it is the saying of al-Murraqqish:

"Every day for her there is a [...], and a prepared kibā', and ḥamīm."

The scalding water of the Fire, as has been reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when the disbeliever brings it near his mouth, the skin of his head falls away, and it is as Allah, exalted is He, described: ﴿It scalds the faces﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 5–6:

(p-451) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stations, that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth. He details the signs for a people who know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in the alternation of the night and the day, and in what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth, are signs for a people who are conscious of Allah.﴾

This is a continuation of the description of the signs of Allah and the drawing of attention to His craftsmanship, which indicates the Maker. This verse requires that ḍiyā' (radiance) be greater than nūr (light) and more brilliant, in accordance with the sun and the moon. An objection arises here: we find that Allah, exalted is He, likened His guidance and His subtle kindness to His creation to light, saying: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. This requires that light be the greatest of these things and the most eloquent in shining. Otherwise, why was the higher comparison, which is radiance, abandoned in favour of the lesser, which is light? The answer to this, and the resolution, is that you say: the word nūr is more precise and more eloquent in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, and are content with the life of this world and at rest in it, and those who are heedless of Our signs,﴾ ﴿their refuge is the Fire because of what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith; rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿Their call therein will be, "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein will be "Peace," and the last of their call will be, "Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

Abu 'Ubayda said, and al-Qutabi and others followed him: "'Yarjuna' (they expect) in this verse means 'yakhafuna' (they fear)." They cited the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

؎ When the bee stings him, he does not expect its sting (to stop),
∗∗∗ and he opposes it in a hive of honey-combs.

Al-Mahdawi related from some of the people of linguistics (Ibn Sidah said it was al-Farra'), that the word *raja'* (expectation), when it comes in negated form, means fear. It is also reported from some of them that it carries its own meaning in every place where the context before and after it indicates that meaning. According to this interpretation, the meaning of the verse is: "Indeed, those who do not fear meeting Us."

Ibn Zayd said: this verse refers to the disbelievers. Some scholars said: *raja'* in this verse keeps its basic meaning, because the disbelieving denier of the Resurrection does not hope for the mercy of Allah in the Hereafter, nor does he have a good opinion that he will meet Allah, nor does he have any hope in the Hereafter. It may also mean that faith itself is the guidance, i.e., He guides them to the paths of Paradise by the light of their faith. Mujahid said: their faith will be a light for them by which they walk. This interpretation is supported by what was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, when the believing servant rises from his grave for the gathering, a man of beautiful face and pleasant scent will appear to him, and he will say: 'Who are you?' This was related by Ibn Jurayj and Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna.

؎ Of all that a young man attains,
∗∗∗ I have attained it, except *al-tahiyya*.

He means people's supplication for kings with life. The king was called *tahiyya* by this extension. From this is also the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

؎ I visit Abu Qabus until
∗∗∗ I make my army kneel at his *tahiyya*.

He meant: at his kingdom. Some scholars said: ﴿and their greeting﴾ means the greeting of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and *al-salam* (peace) is derived from *al-salama* (safety).

؎ Among youths like Indian swords, they know
∗∗∗ that every one who goes barefoot or wears sandals will perish.

﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, and are content with the life of this world and at rest in it, and those who are heedless of Our signs,﴾ ﴿their refuge is the Fire because of what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith; rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿Their call therein will be, "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein will be "Peace," and the last of their call will be, "Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

Abu 'Ubayda said, and al-Qutabi and others followed him: "'Yarjuna' (they expect) in this verse means 'yakhafuna' (they fear)." They cited the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

؎ When the bee stings him, he does not expect its sting (to stop),
∗∗∗ and he opposes it in a hive of honey-combs.

Al-Mahdawi related from some of the people of linguistics (Ibn Sidah said it was al-Farra'), that the word *raja'* (expectation), when it comes in negated form, means fear. It is also reported from some of them that it carries its own meaning in every place where the context before and after it indicates that meaning. According to this interpretation, the meaning of the verse is: "Indeed, those who do not fear meeting Us."

Ibn Zayd said: this verse refers to the disbelievers. Some scholars said: *raja'* in this verse keeps its basic meaning, because the disbelieving denier of the Resurrection does not hope for the mercy of Allah in the Hereafter, nor does he have a good opinion that he will meet Allah, nor does he have any hope in the Hereafter. For if he had hope in it, fear would inevitably accompany that hope, and this state of accompanying fear is the cause of salvation. What I say is that *raja'* in every place keeps its basic meaning, and the verse of the Hudhali (Abu Dhu'ayb) means: he did not expect (relief), since it had stung him; so he builds upon this and endures, knowing that there is no escape from it.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 10, verses 11–12:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿If God were to hasten evil upon people as they hasten for good, their term would surely have been decreed for them. So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ ﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing. But when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as though he had never called upon Us for a harm that touched him. Thus is made attractive to the extravagant what they have been doing.﴾

Mujahid said: "It was revealed concerning a man's supplication against himself, his property, his child, or the like. God, exalted is He, informed that if He were to respond to them with harm in the same way they wish to act toward themselves when responding to good, He would destroy them. Then, after that, He omitted from the speech a clause implied by the outward meaning, its estimated form being: 'And He does not do that, but He leaves those who do not expect.' So the speech was abridged (iqtiḍab), and this meaning was reached through His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us﴾. Reflect on this estimation and you will find it sound. And ﴿istiʿjālahum﴾ (their hastening) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar, infinitive), and the estimation is: 'like their hastening.' It was also said that the estimation is: 'hastening like their hastening,' and this is close to the first."

It was also said that this verse was revealed concerning His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. [p. 458] It was also said that it was revealed concerning His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Bring us what you promise us﴾ [al-A'raf: 77] and what runs in its course.

The majority of reciters read ﴿la-quḍiya﴾ (it would have been decreed) with the verb in the passive and ﴿al-ajal﴾ (the term) in the nominative. Ibn 'Amir alone, along with 'Awf, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and Ya'qub, read ﴿la-qaḍā﴾ with the verb in the active and ﴿al-ajal﴾ in the accusative. Al-A'mash read ﴿la-qaḍaynā﴾ (We would have decreed). The term "al-ajal" in this place means the term of death. The meaning of "qaḍā" (decree, here: complete, finish) in this verse is: completed and finished. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"And upon them both are two coats of mail, woven close, which Dawud (David) finished, or Tubba' the maker of the flowing coats of mail."

Abu 'Ali recited, for this meaning:

"I accomplished affairs, then after them I left fresh buds in their sheaths, not yet opened."

The verb "qaḍā" in this verse takes "ilā" (to), because it has the meaning of "faragha" (to finish), and "faragha" takes "ilā" and also takes "li-" (for). From the former is the saying of Jarir:

"Now I have finished with Numayr, so I have become a torment to its community."

[p. 459] And from the latter is the saying of His, exalted and majestic: ﴿We will be free for you, O you two heavy ones﴾ [al-Rahman: 31]. Al-A'mash read ﴿fa-nadhar alladhina la yarjuna liqa'anā﴾ (So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us). The verb "yarjūn" (they expect) in this place is used in its original sense, and what is meant is those who do not believe in the Resurrection; they do not expect to meet God. Hope (rajā') is always accompanied by fear. "Ṭughyān" (transgression) is excess in a matter and going beyond the limit. "ʿAmah" (wandering blindly) is stumbling about in error.

This verse was revealed as a censure of a blameworthy character that is found among people: they supplicate for good and want the answer hastened, and then bad character sometimes drives them to supplicate for evil. Had He hastened it for them, they would have perished.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿When harm touches man﴾, this verse also is a rebuke for the bad character of some people. Its implication is the prohibition of such conduct and the command to submit to God, exalted is He, and to humble oneself before Him in every state, and the knowledge that good and evil come from Him, and there is no lord other than Him.

His saying "li-janbihi" (lying on his side) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if he had said: "lying down." It is permissible for it to be a ḥāl from "al-insān" (man), with "massa" (touched) as its governing verb, and it is permissible for it to be a ḥāl from the pronoun of the subject in "daʿānā" (called upon Us), with "daʿā" (called) as its governing verb. These are two different meanings.

"Ḍurr" (harm) is a general term for all illnesses and calamities concerning the self, property, and loved ones. This is the view of the lexicographers. It was also said that it is specific to calamities of the body: emaciation and sickness.

His saying "marra" (he passes on) indicates that its revelation concerned the unbelievers. Then, after that, it encompasses everyone who falls under its meaning among the unbeliever or the disobedient. So the meaning of the verse is: he passes on in his associating others with God and his weak reliance upon Him.

His saying "zuyyina" (is made attractive): if we attribute it to God, blessed and exalted is He, then it is His creating disbelief for them and His originating in their souls the companionship of their corrupt deeds and their persistence in them. If we attribute it to the devil (shayṭān), then it means whispering (waswasa) and deception. The word "tazyīn" (making attractive) has come in the Qur'an with both these meanings: once from the act of God, exalted is He, and once from the act of the devils.

(p-460) The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿Indeed, We destroyed the generations before you when they did wrong, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, yet they were not going to believe. Thus do We recompense the criminal people.﴾ ﴿Then We made you successors in the land after them, that We might see how you would act.﴾ ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it." Say: "It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I follow only what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day."﴾

This verse is a threat to the disbelievers and a presenting of examples to them, meaning: just as these people did, so will be done to you what was done to them.

His saying, ﴿and they were not going to believe﴾, is a report about the hardness of their hearts and the severity of their disbelief. The majority of the Seven (readers) and others read "najzī" (نَجْزِي, "We recompense") with the plural "nūn," and a group read "yajzī" (يَجْزِي, "He recompenses") with the "yā'," meaning: God recompenses. "Khalā'if" (خَلائِفُ) is the plural of "khalīfa" (successor). His saying "liyanẓura" (لِنَنْظُرَ, "that We might see") means: that We might make manifest in existence what We had known from eternity, but the statement has come in the manner of concision and eloquence. Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith (a reader) read it, and said: "I saw it in the Imam (the master codex of 'Uthman)," as "liyanẓura" (لِنَظُّرَ) with the "nūn" assimilated into the "ẓā'." 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed, Allah the Exalted only made us successors so that He may see how we act, so display to Allah the goodness of your deeds, both in secret and in public." He also used to say: "You have been made a successor, O son of al-Khaṭṭāb, so see how you act," and at times he would say: "You have been made a successor, O son of Umm 'Umar."

His saying, ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ to the end of the verse: this verse was revealed concerning the Quraysh, because some of their disbelievers said this statement, meaning: "Be lenient with us, O Muhammad, and make this speech that comes from you subject to our choice; permit what you have forbidden and forbid what you have permitted, so that our affair will then be one and our word united." So Allah censured this scheme and reminded them that they say this about the clear verses, and He described them as not believing in the Resurrection. Then Allah commanded His Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, to respond to them with the manifest truth, to submit, to follow the judgment of Allah the Exalted, and to inform his Lord of his fear. The tremendous Day is the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 16–18:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: "Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made you aware of it. I have dwelt among you a lifetime before it. Will you not then reason?"﴾ ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah, or denies His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper.﴾ ﴿They worship, besides Allah, that which neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah." Say: "Will you inform Allah of something He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?" Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

This is from the perfection of the proof. That is: this speech is not from me, nor from my own devising; rather it is from Allah. Had He willed, He would not have sent me with it, nor would I have recited it to you, nor would I have informed you of it. The word ﴿adrākum﴾ means "made you know" (a'lamakum). It is said: "daraytu bil-amr" and "adraytu ghayrī" (I knew of the matter and I made another know it). This is the reading of the majority. Ibn Kathir, in some of what is transmitted from him, read: "wa la-adrākum bihi," where the lām is an emphatic lām that entered upon "adrā," and the meaning in this case is: "and He would certainly have made you know of it by other than my means." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), Ibn Sirin, Abu Raja' and al-Hasan read: "wa lā adra'tukum bihi." Ibn 'Abbas also read, as did Shahr ibn Hawshab: "wa lā andhartukum bihi." Al-Farra' explained the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan as a dialectal usage of some Arabs, among which is their saying "labba'tu" meaning "labbaytu," and the saying of a woman of them: "ra'ath-tu zawjī bi-abyāt," meaning "ra'aytu" (I lamented my husband with verses). Abu al-Fath said: it is in fact "adraytukum," with the yā' changed to an alif because the letter before it has a fatha. It has been related from Qutrub that the dialect of 'Uqayl in "a'taytuka" is "a'ta'tuka." Abu Hatim said: the yā' was changed to an alif as in the dialect of Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b: "as-salāmu 'alāka."

Then He said: ﴿I have dwelt among you a lifetime before it﴾, that is, forty years before his prophethood, peace be upon him. He means: you did not test me in a lie, nor did I speak about anything of this kind. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ that one who has this attribute cannot possibly utter a lie after his age has grown and his hope has become brief, and his judgment and his fear of his Lord have become firm. The majority recite "labith-tu" with clear pronunciation, while Abu 'Amr reads "labit-tu" with the tha' assimilated into the ta'.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who is more unjust﴾ and the rest of the verse, in this verse there is a reproach concerning the enormity of the crime of one who fabricates against Allah after disavowal of that has preceded. It is said: thus the speech is coherent and its eloquence is uniform. His saying ﴿Who is more unjust﴾ is an interrogative of affirmation, meaning: none is more unjust ﴿than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or﴾ than one who ﴿denies His signs﴾ after their clarification. That is the greatest crime against Allah and the most inviting of His punishment. Then He affirmed that the people of crime do not prosper; ﴿yufliḥu﴾ means: attains his aim.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They worship, besides Allah, that which neither harms them nor benefits them﴾ and the rest of the verse, the pronoun in "ya'budūn" refers to the unbelievers of Quraysh whose discourse preceded. ﴿That which neither harms them nor benefits them﴾ refers to the idols. Their saying ﴿These are our intercessors﴾ is the position of their nobles. So Allah commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to affirm this against them and rebuke them: Do they inform Allah of tidings in the heavens and the earth that He Himself does not know? He mentioned "the heavens" because among the Arabs are those who worship the angels and Sirius, and in accordance with this it is fitting to say "these." It was also said that this is by way of metaphor for idols, which do not reason. In this affirmation there is the greatest refutation of them, and they cannot but say: "We do not do it and we are not able to," and that is necessarily implied by their saying: ﴿These are our intercessors﴾. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ is a resumptive phrase of exalting Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read here "ʿammā yushrikūn" with the yā' in the third person, and in two places in al-Nahl, one in al-Rum and one in al-Naml. Abu Hatim mentioned that Nafi', al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ibn al-Qa'qa', Shayba, Humayd, Talha and al-A'mash read it likewise. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read here and in al-Naml only: "tushrikūn" with the tā' in direct address. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the five instances with the tā', and this is the reading of Abu 'Abd al-Rahman.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

Had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord, the matter would have been decided between them concerning that wherein they differ.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah, so wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ ﴿And when We let mankind taste mercy after adversity has touched them, behold, they have a plot against Our signs. Say, "Allah is swifter in plotting." Indeed, Our messengers record what you plot.﴾

A group said: the intended meaning is Adam, who was one community, and then people differed after him, and over the affairs of his sons. Another group said: the intended meaning is the offspring of his sons, when Allah brought them out from his back and made them bear witness against themselves. Another group said: the intended meaning is Adam and his sons from his descent until one of his two sons killed the other. Another group said: the intended meaning is, "Mankind were but one community in error and in ignorance of Allah, then they split into sects regarding that according to the degree of their ignorance." It is also possible that the meaning is: mankind were one kind, prepared for guidance. The full treatment of this has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah, in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Mankind were one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213].

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Shayba and Abu 'Amr recited (p-464) "la-qudiya baynahum" with a damma on the qaf and a kasra on the dad. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "laqada" with a fatha on both, as a past-tense verb.

As for His saying: ﴿And were it not for a word that had preceded from your Lord﴾, it means His decree and determination for the children of Adam with fixed terms of life. It is also possible that it means the word concerning the matter of the Resurrection, and that reward and punishment will only take place at that time.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ and so on, by their saying ﴿a sign from his Lord﴾ they mean a sign that would compel people to faith. This kind of sign no prophet has ever brought, nor are they compelling miracles. Rather, they are offered for examination, so that some people may be guided and others go astray. As for His saying: ﴿Say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah"﴾, He does whatever He wills, and if He wills He does not do it; no one has access to His unseen. As for His saying: ﴿So wait﴾, it is a threat, and Allah, blessed and exalted, has indeed confirmed it by granting victory to Muhammad (ﷺ), as al-Tabari said: at Badr and elsewhere.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We let mankind taste﴾ and so on, the intended meaning of "mankind" in this verse is the disbelievers. It also encompasses, among the disobedient, those who do not render thanks to Allah, blessed and exalted, when the hardship is removed from them, and are not restrained from their sins by that. Such people are numerous among mankind. Mercy here, after adversity, is like rain after drought, security after fear, health after sickness, and similar things that cannot be counted. Makr (plotting) means mockery and slander against it by the disbelievers, and abandoning gratitude and fear by the sinners. Describing Allah's makr as swift, although the gradual leading-on (istidraj) of them is slow, is because it is certain to happen and will inevitably come, and everything that is coming is near. Abu Hatim said: people recited "inna rusulana" with a damma on the sin, while al-Hasan, Ibn Abi al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr lightened the sin.

It is said "asra'" from saraa (sara'a), and it does not come from asra'a yusri'u. Abu 'Ali transmitted this, and said: "If it were from asra'a it would be irregular (shadhdh)."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning the Fire of Jahannam: "It is blacker than pitch." Whatever has been preserved from the Prophet (ﷺ) is not irregular.

Abu Hatim said: Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil said: in the mushaf (codex) of Ubayy, it reads: "O mankind, indeed Allah is swifter in plotting, and indeed His messengers are with you, recording what you plot."

Abu Hatim said: people recited "inna rusulana" with a damma on the sin, while al-Hasan, Ibn Abi al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr lightened the sin.

It is said "asra'" from saraa (sara'a), and it does not come from asra'a yusri'u. Abu 'Ali transmitted this, and said: "If it were from asra'a it would be irregular (shadhdh)."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning the Fire of Jahannam: "It is blacker than pitch." Whatever has been preserved from the Prophet (ﷺ) is not irregular.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Nafi', Qatada and Mujahid recited "tamkuruna" with a ta' in the second person, and this is the reading of the people of Makkah, Shibl, Abu 'Amr, 'Isa, Talha, 'Asim, al-A'mash, al-Jahdari and Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil. [Al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid] also recited it in the third person, "yamkuruna," and this is also transmitted from Nafi' and al-A'raj. Abu Hatim said: Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil said: in the mushaf (codex) of Ubayy, it reads: "O mankind, indeed Allah is swifter in plotting, and indeed His messengers are with you, recording what you plot."

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Mankind were but one community, then they differed. Had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord, the matter would have been decided between them concerning that wherein they differ.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah, so wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ ﴿And when We let mankind taste mercy after adversity has touched them, behold, they have a plot against Our signs. Say, "Allah is swifter in plotting." Indeed, Our messengers record what you plot.﴾

A group said: the intended meaning is Adam, who was one community, and then people differed after him, and over the affairs of his sons. Another group said: the intended meaning is the offspring of his sons, when Allah brought them out from his back and made them bear witness against themselves. Another group said: the intended meaning is Adam and his sons from his descent until one of his two sons killed the other. Another group said: the intended meaning is, "Mankind were but one community in error and in ignorance of Allah, then they split into sects regarding that according to the degree of their ignorance." It is also possible that the meaning is: mankind were one kind, prepared for guidance. The full treatment of this has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah, in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Mankind were one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213].

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Shayba and Abu 'Amr recited (p-464) "la-qudiya baynahum" with a damma on the qaf and a kasra on the dad. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "laqada" with a fatha on both, as a past-tense verb.

As for His saying: ﴿And were it not for a word that had preceded from your Lord﴾, it means His decree and determination for the children of Adam with fixed terms of life. It is also possible that it means the word concerning the matter of the Resurrection, and that reward and punishment will only take place at that time.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ and so on, by their saying ﴿a sign from his Lord﴾ they mean a sign that would compel people to faith. This kind of sign no prophet has ever brought, nor are they compelling miracles. Rather, they are offered for examination, so that some people may be guided and others go astray. As for His saying: ﴿Say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah"﴾, He does whatever He wills, and if He wills He does not do it; no one has access to His unseen. As for His saying: ﴿So wait﴾, it is a threat, and Allah, blessed and exalted, has indeed confirmed it by granting victory to Muhammad (ﷺ), as al-Tabari said: at Badr and elsewhere.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We let mankind taste﴾ and so on, the intended meaning of "mankind" in this verse is the disbelievers. It also encompasses, among the disobedient, those who do not render thanks to Allah, blessed and exalted, when the hardship is removed from them, and are not restrained from their sins by that. Such people are numerous among mankind. Mercy here, after adversity, is like rain after drought, security after fear, health after sickness, and similar things that cannot be counted. Makr (plotting) means mockery and slander against it by the disbelievers, and abandoning gratitude and fear by the sinners. Describing Allah's makr as swift, although the gradual leading-on (istidraj) of them is slow, is because it is certain to happen and will inevitably come, and everything that is coming is near. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning the Fire of Jahannam: "It is blacker than pitch." Whatever has been preserved from the Prophet (ﷺ) is not irregular.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Nafi', Qatada and Mujahid recited "tamkuruna" with a ta' in the second person, and this is the reading of the people of Makkah, Shibl, Abu 'Amr, 'Isa, Talha, 'Asim, al-A'mash, al-Jahdari and Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil. [Al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid] also recited it in the third person, "yamkuruna," and this is also transmitted from Nafi' and al-A'raj. Abu Hatim said: Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil said: in the mushaf (codex) of Ubayy, it reads: "O mankind, indeed Allah is swifter in plotting, and indeed His messengers are with you, recording what you plot."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 22:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea, until when you are in ships and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice therein, there comes a violent wind and the waves come to them from everywhere and they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion: "If You should save us from this, we will surely be among the grateful."﴾

This verse includes enumerating the blessing in the state of riding the sea. Riding it in calm conditions, for jihad and Hajj, is agreed to be permissible. Likewise, it is permissible out of necessity for livelihood through fishing in it, or for conducting trade. As for riding it in pursuit of wealth and increasing one's gains, it is disliked according to most scholars, and the most that can be said in permitting it is that abandoning it is better. As for riding it when it is turbulent (irtijaj), it is disliked and forbidden. In a hadith: "Whoever rides the sea when it is turbulent, the protection (dhimmah) of God is absolved from him."

(p-٤٦٦) The Prophet ﷺ said: "I will never ride the sea."

The majority of the reciters among the Seven and others recited: "yusayyirukum" (enables you to travel). Abu 'Ali said: This is the intensive doubling (ta'diyah mubalaghah) of the verb, not the transitive doubling (ta'diyah ta'diyah), because the Arabs say: "sirtu al-rajula" and "sayyartuhu" (I traveled him / I made him travel). From this is the saying of the Hudhali poet:

"So do not grieve over a way of life that you yourself have followed,
for the first to be content with a practice is the one who follows it."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is an objection to this line, so that it does not serve as evidence for this point, namely that the pronoun is treated like an adverb of place, as when you say: "sirtu al-tariqa" (I traveled the road). This is the reading of the majority from "sayara," and it is likewise in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud and in the codex of Abi Shaykh. 'Awf ibn Abi Jamila said: (p-٤٦٧) He used to recite "yanshurukum" (spreads you out), but al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf changed it to "yusayyirukum." Sufyan ibn Abi al-Zaal said: They used to recite "yanshurukum," then they looked in the codex of Ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, and found it to be "yusayyirukum." The first to write it that way was al-Hajjaj.

Ibn Kathir in some of his transmissions recited "yusirukum" from "asara." Ibn 'Amir alone among the Seven recited "yanshurukum" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the shin, from al-nashr wa al-bath (spreading and scattering). This is the reading of Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu Ja'far, 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr ibn al-Fasih, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and Shayba. It is narrated from al-Hasan that he recited "yunshirukum" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the shin, and he said it is the reading of 'Abdullah. Abu Hatim said: I think he made a mistake.

"Al-fulk" is the plural of "fulk," and it is not a singular noun used for both the plural and the singular. Rather, it is a form (fu'l) pluralized on the pattern fu'l. What indicates this is their saying "fulkan" in the dual. The reading of Abu al-Darda' and Umm al-Darda' is "fi al-fulkiyy," on the pattern fu'liyy with the ya' of relative attribution, as in their saying "ashqariyy" and "dawwariyy" (of the wheel) in "dawr al-dahr," and like the saying of al-Salatan:

"I am al-Salatani..."

(p-٤٦٨) His saying "wa jarayna" (and they sailed) is a marker of small number (the dual/few form). His saying "bihim" (with them) is a shift from address (the second person) to the third person absent. This is fine because their saying "kuntum fi al-fulk" (when you are in the ships) is in the intelligible sense, until some of you are in the boats. When "al-rih" (wind) appears in the singular, its customary usage is for punishment and what is disliked. But in the sea it is not fitting for it to be anything other than a single wind, not a plural of winds. So the singular is qualified with "tayyib" (good), and it departs from that custom and the meaning is perfected.

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "ja'atbhum rihun 'asifun" (a violent wind came upon them). "Al-'asif" is the strong wind; it is said: "'asafat al-rih" (the wind blew violently).

His saying "wa zannu" (and they thought) is in its ordinary sense of thinking, but it is a dominant thought, frightening, because they are in a feared situation.

His saying "da'awu Allah" (they called upon Allah) means: they forgot the idols and the partners, and they devoted their supplication exclusively to Allah. Al-Tabari mentioned on the authority of some scholars the report of the saying of the non-Arabs: "Hayya shara-hiya," and its meaning: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting." Al-Tabari said: The response to His saying "until when you are in the ships and they sailed" is "there came upon them a violent wind," and the response to His saying "and they thought they were encompassed" is "they called upon Allah, sincere."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 23:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then when He had delivered them, behold, they committed outrage in the earth without right. O mankind, your outrage is only against yourselves; it is the enjoyment of the life of this world. Then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

"Yabghūna" (they commit outrage): i.e., they corrupt and disbelieve. Al-baghy (outrage) is transgression and corrupt deeds. He emphasized this (p-469) by His saying: ﴿without right﴾. Then He began with rebuke and condemnation of outrage in the most concise wording. His saying "matā'u al-ḥayāh" (the enjoyment of life) is in the nominative case (rafʿ), and this is the reading of the majority. This is on the basis of the predicate of the inchoative, the subject being "baghyukum" (your outrage). It is also permissible for "matā'" to be nominative as the predicate of an implied inchoative, its estimated form being: "that is an enjoyment," or "it is an enjoyment." The predicate of "al-baghy" is His saying: "ʿalā anfusikum" (against yourselves). Ḥafs, from ʿĀṣim, and Hārūn, from Ibn Kathīr, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read "matā'a" with the accusative, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) relating to "al-baghy." In this case, the predicate of "al-baghy" is omitted, its estimated form being: "blameworthy" or "detestable" or something similar. It is not permissible for the predicate to be His saying "ʿalā anfusikum," because this would place a foreign element between the verbal noun and what it governs. It is also permissible for "matā'a" to be in the accusative by an implied verb, its estimated form being: "you are given the enjoyment of the life of this world." Ibn Abī Isḥāq read "matā'an al-ḥayāh al-dunyā" with the accusative in both places. The meaning of the verse: your outrage and corruption are only harmful to you; it is in the state of this world, then you will meet its punishment in the Hereafter. Sufyān ibn 'Uyayna said: ﴿Your outrage is only against yourselves; it is the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾, i.e., its punishment is hastened for you in the life of this world. On this basis they said: outrage throws its people down.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They also said: the one who commits outrage is overthrown, based on His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Then whoever is wronged, Allah will surely help him﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 60], and on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No sin is more quickly punished than outrage." A group read "fa-nunabbi'ukum" as the first person plural, referring to the Majestic Speaker, and a group read "fa-yunabbi'ukum" as the third person, the intended meaning being Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 24:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, the likeness of the worldly life is like water which We sent down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingled with it, of what men and livestock eat, until when the earth took on its adornment and was beautified, and its people thought they had power over it, Our command came to it by night or by day, and We made it a harvested field, as though it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We detail the signs for a people who give thought.﴾

The meaning: indeed, the likeness of the boastfulness of the worldly life and its adornment with wealth and children, as that ends in annihilation, is like rain that descended from the sky and mingled. Some reciters paused here on the meaning "the water mingled with the earth," then resumed with ﴿bihi nabatu al-ard﴾ ("by it, the plants of the earth") as an inchoate clause with a preposed predicate (ibtida' wa-khabar muqaddam). On this reading, the pronoun in "bihi" may refer back to the water or to the mingling (al-ikhtilat) implied by the statement. Another group connected the phrase, and so "al-nabat" (the plants) was read in the nominative as the subject of "fakhtalata" (mingled), meaning: the plants mingled, some of them with others, by means of the water. His saying ﴿of what men eat﴾ means crops, trees and the like, and His saying ﴿and livestock﴾ means the rest of the pasture grass.

﴿Akhadhat al-ard﴾ ("the earth took") is an expression frequently used in such contexts, like His saying ﴿Take your adornment﴾ [al-A'raf: 31]. Al-zukhruf means adornment with colours, and zukhruf may also mean gold, since gold is among it. Marwan ibn al-Hakam, Abu Ja'far, the Seven, Shayba, Mujahid and the majority read ﴿wazzayyanat﴾; its origin is "tazayyanat," the ta' was made quiescent in order to assimilate it, and so a hamzat al-wasl was needed. Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read ﴿wa-tazayyanat﴾, and this is the origin of the majority reading. al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Sha'bi, Qatada, Nasr ibn 'Asim and 'Isa read ﴿wa-azyanat﴾, meaning its adornment appeared, as one says "ahsada al-zar'u" (the crop was harvested), and "azyanat" follows the pattern of "af'alat." 'Awf ibn Abi Jamila said: "Our shaykhs used to read it: 'wazayyanat,'" with the nun shadda and the alif quiescent before it; this is the reading of Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi. A group read "wazay'annat," which is a dialect form, as in the poet's verse:

...................... ∗∗∗ when the flocks of the herds were mixed with fresh blood (ihmarrat)

A group read "wazzaynat" (wazzayanat) in the form "wazza'yanat." The meaning in all of this is: its adornment became manifest.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and its people thought﴾ is on its own basis. The pronoun in "'alayha" refers to the earth, and what is meant is what is in it of blessing and vegetation. This statement contains a comparison of the whole matter of the worldly life with this described state. "Hatta" is a limit (ghayah), and it is a particle of inception because it is followed by "idha"; its sense continues up to His saying ﴿able to master it﴾, and the answer begins after that. The coming command is one of the affairs, such as wind, frost, scorching wind and the like. Its division into "by night or by day" is an alert to fear and to the absence of security at every time. "Hasidan" is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and by "hasid" he expressed the destroyed, perished vegetation, even if it was not destroyed by harvesting, since the ruling for both is one, and as if the blight had reaped it before its time. His saying ﴿as though it had not flourished﴾ means: as though it had not been pleasant, nor fresh, nor shown itself in its lushness. Qatada read "yaghna" with a ya' from below, meaning the harvested crop. Marwan read "ka'an lam tatagHanna" with two ta's, like "tatafa''ala." And al-maghani are inhabited dwellings; from it is the poet's verse:

And we have dwelt in them and seen ages ∗∗∗ in which they lured us, the tender, slender maidens.

In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "as though it had not flourished yesterday," and "We did not destroy it except for the sins of its people" ... "thus do We detail the signs," which Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, narrated from him. It was also said that in it is: "And Allah would not have destroyed it except for the sins of its people." Abu al-Darda' read: "for a people who remember."

The meaning of the verse is a warning against being deceived by the world, since it is exposed to perishing, and that there may befall it what befell this mentioned land, by death or other calamities of the world. He singled out those who reflect for mention, to honour their station, and so that the race to this rank may take place.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 25–27:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying:

﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace, and guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾ ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward), and more. Neither darkness nor humiliation shall cover their faces. Those are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿But those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like, and humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah. It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the darkness of night. Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾

This verse indicates that the calling to the Law (al-shar') is general to all humankind, while guidance, which is direction (al-irshad), is specific to those whose faith has been decreed. As for "al-Salam" (the Peace), it is said that it is a name of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, so the meaning is that He calls to His abode, which is the Garden, and its attribution to Him is an attribution of ownership to the owner. It is also said that "al-Salam" means "safety," i.e., whoever enters it attains safety and is secure from perishing and calamities. This verse is a refutation of the Mu'tazila (a theological school).

Traditions have been related about Allah's calling of His servants, among them the Prophet's (ﷺ) vision of Jibril and Mika'il, in which they represented Allah's call, Muhammad (ﷺ) as the caller, the religion to which he calls, and the Garden, which is the fruit of forgiveness, as a feast to which a king invites people to his house. Qatada, in his discourse on this verse, mentioned: "It has been related to us that in the Torah it is written: 'O seeker of good, come (halumma); and O seeker of evil, desist.'"

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward), and more.﴾ (the verse), one group, and they are the majority, said: "The best (husna) is the Garden, and the increase (ziyada) is the gazing upon the Face of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic." A tradition to this effect has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ), narrated by Suhayb. This view has also been related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Hudhayfa, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Amir ibn Sa'd, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla. It is also related from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The increase is one pearl chamber."

Another group said: "The best (husna) is the good deed (hasana), and the increase is the multiplication of good deeds up to seven hundred (times) or less, as related in the text of the hadith, and (this is) the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqara: 261]." This view is supported by reasoning, and were it not for the eminence of those who hold the first view, this view would be preferred. The way to prefer it is that the verse includes a pairing between the mention of the doers of good deeds and the doers of evil deeds. It describes the good-doers as having, for their goodness, a best reward and an increase of the same kind, and it describes the evil-doers as having for an evil deed its like, so the two statements are balanced. He expressed the good deeds as "the best" (husna) as an intensification, since they are ten (times). Al-Tabari said: "The husna is general to every kind of good, so it encompasses all that has been said, and Allah, the Exalted, promised an increase in all of them." This is also supported by His saying: ﴿Those are the companions of the Garden﴾, for if the meaning of husna were the Garden, the statement would contain a repetition in meaning. Yet this can be answered by saying that it describes the good-doers as having the Garden, and that they will not be covered by darkness or humiliation; then He said: ﴿Those are the companions of the Garden﴾ by way of praising them, meaning: those are its deserving and rightful companions, by right and by merit.

"Yarhaqu" means: it covers with humiliation and constriction. "Qatar" is blackened dust, and from it is the poet's saying:

Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, in the midst of which you see the banners and the dust.

Al-Hasan, Isa ibn Umar, al-A'mash, and Abu Raja read "qatrun" with a sukun on the ta'. As for His saying: ﴿But those who earned evil deeds﴾ (the verse), the grammarians differed concerning the grammatical basis of the nominative case of "al-jaza'" (the recompense): what does it depend on? One group said: the estimated (sense) is: "for them is the recompense of an evil deed by its like," and another group said: the estimated (sense) is: "the recompense of an evil deed is its like," with the "ba'" being superfluous.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is plausible that the nominative "al-jaza'" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in "alladhina" (those who), because "wa-alladhina" is conjoined to His saying "li-alladhina ahsanu" (for those who did good), so it is as if He said: "And for those who earned evil deeds is the recompense of an evil deed by its like." On the other reading, His saying ﴿But those who earned evil deeds﴾ is nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and the evil deeds here encompass disbelief and disobedience. The like of the evil deed of disbelief is eternal abiding in the Fire, and the like of the evil deed of disobedience is left to the will of Allah, blessed and exalted.

"Al-'Asim" is the one who saves and protects, and from it is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾ [Hud: 43]. "Ughshiyat" means: was clothed, and from it comes "al-ghishawa" (covering). "Qita'" is the plural of "qit'a" (piece). Ibn Kathir read "qit'an" with a sukun on the ta', and the rest read it with a fatha on the ta'. "Al-qit'" is a portion of the night, and from it is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿So travel with your family in a part of the night﴾ [al-Hijr: 65]. Here it is intended as a portion of the time of the night, while in this verse it is a portion of its darkness. "Muzliman" is an attribute (na't) of "qit'an," and it may be a circumstantial (hal) clause from the mention in His saying "min al-layl" (of the night). If it is an attribute, its proper place would be before the clause, but it may come after it, and the estimated clause is: "a piece that settled from the night, dark," in the manner of His, blessed and exalted, saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ [al-An'am: 155]. As for the one who reads "qita'an" as the plural of "qit'a," the accusative of "muzliman" is as a circumstantial clause from "al-layl," and the governing element of the circumstantial clause is "min," since it is the governing element of the one in the circumstance. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "ka'anna yughsha wujuhahum qit'un min al-layli muzlimun," and Ibn Abi Abla read: "qita'un min al-layli muzlimun," with the ta' of "qita'in" vowelled.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward), and more.﴾ (the verse), one group, and they are the majority, said: "The best (husna) is the Garden, and the increase (ziyada) is the gazing upon the Face of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic." A tradition to this effect has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ), narrated by Suhayb. This view has also been related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Hudhayfa, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Amir ibn Sa'd, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla. It is also related from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The increase is one pearl chamber."

Another group said: "The best (husna) is the good deed (hasana), and the increase is the multiplication of good deeds up to seven hundred (times) or less, as related in the text of the hadith, and (this is) the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqara: 261]." This view is supported by reasoning, and were it not for the eminence of those who hold the first view, this view would be preferred. The way to prefer it is that the verse includes a pairing between the mention of the doers of good deeds and the doers of evil deeds. It describes the good-doers as having, for their goodness, a best reward and an increase of the same kind, and it describes the evil-doers as having for an evil deed its like, so the two statements are balanced. He expressed the good deeds as "the best" (husna) as an intensification, since they are ten (times). Al-Tabari said: "The husna is general to every kind of good, so it encompasses all that has been said, and Allah, the Exalted, promised an increase in all of them." This is also supported by His saying: ﴿Those are the companions of the Garden﴾, for if the meaning of husna were the Garden, the statement would contain a repetition in meaning. Yet this can be answered by saying that it describes the good-doers as having the Garden, and that they will not be covered by darkness or humiliation; then He said: ﴿Those are the companions of the Garden﴾ by way of praising them, meaning: those are its deserving and rightful companions, by right and by merit.

"Yarhaqu" means: it covers with humiliation and constriction. "Qatar" is blackened dust, and from it is the poet's saying:

Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, in the midst of which you see the banners and the dust.

Al-Hasan, Isa ibn Umar, al-A'mash, and Abu Raja read "qatrun" with a sukun on the ta'. As for His saying: ﴿But those who earned evil deeds﴾ (the verse), the grammarians differed concerning the grammatical basis of the nominative case of "al-jaza'" (the recompense): what does it depend on? One group said: the estimated (sense) is: "for them is the recompense of an evil deed by its like," and another group said: the estimated (sense) is: "the recompense of an evil deed is its like," with the "ba'" being superfluous.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is plausible that the nominative "al-jaza'" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in "alladhina" (those who), because "wa-alladhina" is conjoined to His saying "li-alladhina ahsanu" (for those who did good), so it is as if He said: "And for those who earned evil deeds is the recompense of an evil deed by its like." On the other reading, His saying ﴿But those who earned evil deeds﴾ is nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and the evil deeds here encompass disbelief and disobedience. The like of the evil deed of disbelief is eternal abiding in the Fire, and the like of the evil deed of disobedience is left to the will of Allah, blessed and exalted.

"Al-'Asim" is the one who saves and protects, and from it is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾ [Hud: 43]. "Ughshiyat" means: was clothed, and from it comes "al-ghishawa" (covering). "Qita'" is the plural of "qit'a" (piece). Ibn Kathir read "qit'an" with a sukun on the ta', and the rest read it with a fatha on the ta'. Here it is intended as a portion of the time of the night, while in this verse it is a portion of its darkness. "Muzliman" is an attribute (na't) of "qit'an," and it may be a circumstantial (hal) clause from the mention in His saying "min al-layl" (of the night). If it is an attribute, its proper place would be before the clause, but it may come after it, and the estimated clause is: "a piece that settled from the night, dark," in the manner of His, blessed and exalted, saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ [al-An'am: 155]. As for the one who reads "qita'an" as the plural of "qit'a," the accusative of "muzliman" is as a circumstantial clause from "al-layl," and the governing element of the circumstantial clause is "min," since it is the governing element of the one in the circumstance. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "ka'anna yughsha wujuhahum qit'un min al-layli muzlimun," and Ibn Abi Abla read: "qita'un min al-layli muzlimun," with the ta' of "qita'in" vowelled.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 28–30:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And [mention] the Day We will gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah, "Stay in your place, you and your partners." Then We will separate them, and their partners will say, "You did not used to worship us."﴾ ﴿So Allah suffices as a witness between us and you; indeed, we were unaware of your worship.﴾ ﴿There, every soul will [come to] know what it sent forth, and they will be returned to Allah, their true Master, and lost from them is what they used to invent.﴾

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, al-Hasan, Shayba and others recited "naḥshuruhum" with the nun, while a group recited "yaḥshuruhum" with the ya'. The pronoun in "naḥshuruhum" refers to all people, both the righteous and the wicked. "Makanakum" is in the accusative, under the implied construction: "Remain in your place" (lāzimū makānakum), and this is accompanied by a state of severity and humiliation. "Makanakum" in this place is among the nouns functioning as verbs (asmā' al-af'āl), since its meaning is: "Stand and remain." This is a report from Allah, exalted is He, about a state that will befall the worshippers of idols on the Day of Resurrection, when they are commanded to remain in the place of humiliation together with their idols. Then Allah will cause the idols to speak, disavowing them. His saying "and your partners" means: those whom you claim to be partners of Allah. He attributed them to them because their being partners is only by the claim of these people. His saying "fa-zayyalnā baynahum" means: We separated them in argument and doctrine; it is from ziltu al-shay' 'an al-shay' (I removed a thing from another thing), and it is the intensive doubling (ta'diyya mubālagha), not transitive doubling. The verbal noun of zayyala being tazyīlan indicates that zayyala is fa''ala and not fay'ala, since its verbal noun would come in the form fay'ala. A group recited "fa-zāyalnā" (fa-zāyalnā). It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "When the disbelievers see the punishment and their means are cut off, it will be said to them: 'Follow what you used to worship.' They will say: 'We used to worship these.' The idols will say: 'By Allah, we did not hear nor comprehend, and you did not used to worship us.' They will say: 'By Allah, it is you whom we used to worship.' Then the deities will say: ﴿So Allah suffices as a witness.﴾"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of this verse is that their address is only with the idols, not with the angels or 'Isa ibn Maryam, as evidenced by the saying to them: "Stay in your place, you and your partners," and not with Pharaoh or those among the jinn who were worshipped, as evidenced by their saying: "we were unaware of your worship," and these never at any time were unaware of the worship of those who worshipped them. "Antum" is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is: "reproached" (muwabbakhūn) or "humiliated" (muhānūn). It is also permissible for "antum" to be an emphasis (ta'kīd) for the pronoun in the implied verb, which is "qifū" (stand) or something similar.

"Shahīdan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), and it is said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The "in" here, according to Sibawayh, is the lightened (mukhaffafa) affirmative particle, a particle of beginning, and the lām became attached to it to distinguish it from the negating "in." Al-Farra' said: "in" is in the sense of "mā" and the lām is in the sense of "illā." "Hunālika" is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir recited "tablū" with one ba' meaning "tests," while Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "tatlū" with two dots above, meaning "follows," i.e., seeks and pursues what it sent forth of its deeds. It may also be correct that it means "reads its books which are presented to it." Yahya ibn Wathhab recited "wa-ridduu" with a kasra on the ra', while the majority recited "wa-ruddū ilā Allāh," i.e., they are returned to the punishment of their Owner and the severity of His might. So He is their Master (mawlāhum) in dominion and encompassing power, not in mercy and victory or the like.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 31–33:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who owns hearing and sight? And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living? And who arranges the affair?" They will say, "Allah." So say, "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ ﴿So that is Allah, your Lord, the Truth. So what is there after the truth except error? So how are you turned away?﴾ ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has come into effect against those who defied, that they will not believe.﴾

This is a demand for acknowledgment, a rebuke and an argument from which there is no escape. "From the heaven" means the rain, and "and the earth" means by causing growth and the like. "Who owns hearing and sight" is a expression that encompasses the whole of the human being and most of him, to the extent that whatever else is beyond these two is subordinate. "Brings the living out of the dead" refers to the fetus from the drop of semen, the bird from the egg, and plants from the earth, since they have a growth resembling life. "And brings the dead out of the living" is like the egg from the bird and the like. The full discussion of these meanings has already been given earlier. "Arranges the affair" is general to this and to other than it, among all things, and that is the rectitude of all affairs by His will, the Mighty and Majestic. His arranging is not by thought, deliberation, or changing states, exalted is He above that; rather, His knowledge is all-encompassing, complete and everlasting. "They will say, 'Allah'" — they have no escape from that, and slander by other than Him is not possible for them. When they acknowledge this, "so say, 'Will you not then fear Him?'" — for your fabrication and your making idols into gods.

As for His saying, the Exalted: "So that is Allah, your Lord…" — the verse says: So this One whose attributes these are is your Lord, the Truth, that is, the one deserving worship and divinity. If that is so, then associating others with Him is error and not truth. The expression of the Qur'an in conveying these meanings surpasses every commentary in eloquence, brevity and clarity. This verse decides that between truth and error there is no third position in this matter, which is the Oneness of Allah. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 34–36:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: "Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?" Say: "Allah originates creation and then repeats it. So how are you deluded?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?" Say: "Allah guides to the truth. Is He who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who does not find guidance unless he is guided? What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"﴾ ﴿Most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾

This is also a reproach concerning the deficiency and impotence of the idols, and a reminder of the power of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic. "Beginning of creation" here means bringing man into existence at the first, and "repeating it" is the resurrection from the graves. "Tu'fakun" (you are turned away) means: you are diverted and deprived. The Arabs say "ardun ma'fukah" (a land that has not received rain), meaning it is in a state of failure and inversion, as He said: ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53].

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Say: "Is there any of your partners who guides"﴾ and the verse, "guides to the truth" means: it clarifies the paths of correctness, calls to justice, makes the signs clear, and the like. He described the idols as not guiding unless they are guided, while we find them not being guided even when guided. The explanation of this is that in speaking of them He treated them as they treat them, by describing them with attributes of those who reason; this is a metaphor (majaz) and is found in much of the Qur'an. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi mentioned this. What I say is: the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i allows the meaning: "Or who does not guide anyone unless that one is guided by guidance from Allah." As for the other readings, whose implication is "or who does not find guidance unless he is guided," the meaning is consistent with what Abu 'Ali al-Farisi stated, and in it there is much figurative usage. Some of them said: it is an expression that they do not move unless they are moved. It is also possible that what Allah, the Exalted, mentioned of the glorification of inanimate things is their being guided, and it is possible that the exception concerns their guidance to disowning the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, as has passed in this surah.

The reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i is "yahdi" with a fatha on the ya' and sukun on the ha'. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Shaybah, al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read "yahuddi" with sukun on the ha' and shaddah on the dal. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "yahaddi" with fatha on the ya' and the ha', and this is the most eloquent of the readings: the vowel of the ta' of "yahtadi" was transferred to the ha', and the ta' was assimilated into the dal; this is the transmission of Warsh from Nafi'. 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "yahiddi" with fatha on the ya', kasra on the ha' and shaddah on the dal, making the kasra follow the kasra. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "yihiddi" with kasra on the ya' and the ha' and shaddah on the dal, and this too is assimilation. Mujahid said: Allah guides from the idols and others whomever He wills.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak.

Yahya ibn al-Harith al-Zimari read: "illa an yahaddi" with fatha on the ha' and shaddah on the dal. The reciters paused at "fa-ma lakum," then begin again with "kayfa tahkumun."

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture﴾, it is a report about the corruption of their ways and the weakness of their reasoning, and that it is mere conjecture. Then He explained the status of conjecture among the forms of knowledge and its remoteness from the truth. Conjecture, in this verse, is in its usual sense: it is the belief in one of two permissible possibilities, but there is an inclination toward one of them without proof that refutes the other; and the permissibility of what these people believe is only by their own claim, not in itself. Rather, their conjecture is impossible in its very nature. Truth too is in its usual sense: it is the knowledge of the known as it is. With these conditions, conjecture avails nothing against the truth. As for the paths of rulings which people are obligated to follow by their apparent meanings, conjecture does avail in those realities and is turned from one path to another. Testimony is indeed based on conjecture, and likewise accusations (tuhum) in testimonies are effective. The intent of this verse is not this kind. The majority of people read "yaf'alun." 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read "taf'alun" with the ta', addressing the present audience.
