Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 37–38:

(p-481) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿This Qur'an could not have been fabricated apart from Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you should be truthful."﴾

This is a negation of the saying of some of the Quraysh: "Muhammad (ﷺ) fabricates the Qur'an and attributes it to Allah, the Exalted." He expressed this with these words, which contain a denunciation of their statement and an magnification of the matter, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to deceive﴾ [Al 'Imran: 161], and as He said, relating from 'Isa (peace be upon him): ﴿It is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and other than this, which conveys the meaning, the indications and the proofs of its impossibility.

"Yuftara" means: is invented and originated. It is as if a person fabricates it from his speech, i.e., cuts it off and marks it with a mark; it is derived from "faraytu" when you cut for repair. "Tasdiqa" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), its governing verb being an implied verb. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the predicate of an implied "kana," and the estimate is: "But it was a confirmation of what was before it." His saying, ﴿what is before it﴾, means: the Torah and the Gospel. What is "between the hands" is what precedes a thing. A group said regarding this verse that what is "before it" refers to the portents of the Hour and the matters that will come.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an error, and the matter is the reverse: the Book of Allah, blessed and exalted, is before those. As for al-Zajjaj, he was cautious and said: "The pronoun returns to the portents, and the estimate is: 'But it was a confirmation of what is before the Qur'an.'" This too is unsound. The establishment of proof against the Quraysh at that time was only in that the Qur'an confirms what is in the Torah and the Gospel, while the one who brought the Qur'an is one of whom they are certain did not study those books, nor were they in his land or among his people. "Tafsil al-Kitab" is its clarification. "La rayba fihi" means: it is in itself in this state, and if a deceiver doubts, that is not to be paid heed.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"﴾, the verse, "am" here is not the one that equates with the interrogative alif (p-482) found in your saying: "Did Zayd stand or 'Amr?" Rather, it is the one that occurs in the middle of speech. The position of Sibawayh is that it is like the "alif" and "bal," because it contains interrogation and a turning away from what preceded it, as in their saying: "Is it camels or sheep?" A group said that this "am" is in the position of the interrogative alif. Then He rendered them incapable in His saying: ﴿Say, "Then bring a surah like it"﴾. "Surah" is derived from "surat al-bina'" (the rank of a building), and it is that portion of the Qur'an which has a beginning and an end. The challenge in this verse fell upon both aspects of the inimitability found in the Qur'an: first, the composition, arrangement, conciseness and eloquence, all of which are in describing realities; second, the meanings concerning the unseen regarding what has passed and what is to come. When He challenged them with ten fabricated surahs, He challenged them only with the composition alone.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the saying of a group of the theologians, and in it, in my view, there is an issue. How can the challenge be with a similarity in the unseen matters in response to their saying, "He has invented it"? The challenge in the two verses—this one and the verse of the ten surahs—was only with the composition, arrangement and conciseness in describing realities, and they were never obligated to bring the unseen. For the challenge with the announcement of unseen matters, like His saying: ﴿And they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾ [al-Rum: 3], and His saying: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and similar unseen matters of the Qur'an, it is clear that the human is deficient in that. (p-481) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿This Qur'an could not have been fabricated apart from Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? This is a negation of the saying of some of the Quraysh: "Muhammad (ﷺ) fabricates the Qur'an and attributes it to Allah, the Exalted." He expressed this with these words, which contain a denunciation of their statement and an magnification of the matter, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to deceive﴾ [Al 'Imran: 161], and as He said, relating from 'Isa (peace be upon him): ﴿It is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and other than this, which conveys the meaning, the indications and the proofs of its impossibility.

"Yuftara" means: is invented and originated. It is as if a person fabricates it from his speech, i.e., cuts it off and marks it with a mark; it is derived from "faraytu" when you cut for repair. "Tasdiqa" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), its governing verb being an implied verb. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the predicate of an implied "kana," and the estimate is: "But it was a confirmation of what was before it." His saying, ﴿what is before it﴾, means: the Torah and the Gospel. What is "between the hands" is what precedes a thing. A group said regarding this verse that what is "before it" refers to the portents of the Hour and the matters that will come.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an error, and the matter is the reverse: the Book of Allah, blessed and exalted, is before those. As for al-Zajjaj, he was cautious and said: "The pronoun returns to the portents, and the estimate is: 'But it was a confirmation of what is before the Qur'an.'" This too is unsound. Rather, it is the one that occurs in the middle of speech. The position of Sibawayh is that it is like the "alif" and "bal," because it contains interrogation and a turning away from what preceded it, as in their saying: "Is it camels or sheep?" When He challenged them with ten fabricated surahs, He challenged them only with the composition alone.

(p-484) The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Nay, they denied that of which they had no knowledge, and its interpretation has not yet come to them. Likewise did those before them deny; so see how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it. And your Lord knows best the corrupters.﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my work, and for you is your work. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do."﴾ ﴿And among them are those who listen to you. But can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand?﴾ ﴿And among them are those who look at you. But can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?﴾

The meaning: The matter is not as they say, that it is fabricated. ﴿Nay, they denied that of which they had no knowledge﴾. This wording admits of two meanings. The first is that it refers to the threat which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has promised them for disbelief, and "its interpretation" here means what its matter will come to (its outcome), as in His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but its interpretation?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]. The whole verse, on this interpretation, contains a threat. The second meaning is that He intended: "Nay, they denied this glorious Qur'an, which informs of the unseen, and for which no knowledge had come to them beforehand, nor had they comprehended the knowledge of its unseen matters and the excellence of its composition, nor had the explanation and clarification of that come to them." ﴿Those before them﴾ refers to those of the earlier nations of the prophets. Al-Zajjaj said: "kayfa" (how) is in the position of accusative as the predicate of "kana" (was), and "fanzur" (so see) cannot govern it, because what precedes an interrogative does not govern it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the rule of the grammarians, for they treated "kayfa" everywhere as a pure interrogative, as in your saying: "How is Zayd?" But "kayfa" has usages other than this, where it takes the place of a verbal noun meaning "manner" (kayfiyya) and sheds the sense of interrogation, and this may be one of them. Among its usages is their saying: "Be however you wish (kun kayfa shi'ta)." Consider also al-Bukhari's phrase: "How the beginning of revelation was," for he did not intend a question. (p-485) The verb attributed to "the outcome" (al-'aqiba) is masculine because it carries the sense of "the final return" (al-ma'al) and the like, and its feminine form is not a true feminine.

As for His saying: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it﴾, the pronoun in "minhum" refers to Quraysh. This statement has two meanings. One group said: its meaning is: among these people are those who will believe in the future, and among them are those for whom Allah has decreed that they will never believe. And among them are those who are not believers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The benefit of the verse, on this interpretation, is the dispersal of the unbelievers' word, the weakening of their souls, and that some of them should be apprehensive of others. In His saying: ﴿And your Lord knows best the corrupters﴾ there is a warning and a threat.

His saying: ﴿And if they deny you﴾ is a verse of disengagement and separation from them, and within it is a threat and warning. Many of the exegetes, among them Ibn Zayd, said: this verse is abrogated by fighting, since this surah is Meccan. This is correct.

His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾: He made "yastami'un" (listen) plural in accordance with the meaning of "man" (those), not its wording. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 44–46:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but it is the people who wrong themselves.﴾ ﴿And the Day He gathers them, [it will be] as if they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognizing one another. Those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost, and they were not [rightly] guided.﴾ ﴿And whether We show you part of what We promise them or We take you in death, to Us is their return; then Allah is Witness over what they do.﴾

A group read: "وَلَكِنِ الناسُ" with the lightened "لَكِنْ" (lakin, "but") and the raising of "الناسُ" (al-nās, "the people"), and a group read "وَلَكِنَّ" with the emphatic (tashdid) and the accusative "الناسَ". The wronging of the people of their own selves is only through the acquisition (al-takassub, "acquiring", i.e. the human choice) from them, which accompanies Allah the Exalted's origination (ikhtira', "bringing into being") of their actions. The convention for "لَكِنَّ" (lakinna, "but") is that when a waw ("and") precedes it, it is made heavy (tuthaqqal), and when it is free of waw, it is made light (tukhaffaf); and this rule is sometimes broken. The Kufans said: the lam may enter the predicate of the emphatic "لَكِنَّ" in the same manner as its entry into "إنَّ" (inna), but the Basrans prohibited that.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And the Day He gathers them﴾ to the end of the verse, is a warning of the gathering and of their disgrace therein, and of their mutual cooperation in blaming one another. "يَوْمَ" (yawma, "the day") is an adverbial of time, and its accusative may be governed by a implied verb whose estimate is: "and mention the day", and it may be governed by the verb implied in His statement: ﴿as if they had not remained but an hour of the day﴾, and it may be governed by "يَتَعارَفُونَ" (yatacarafūna, "recognizing one another"). The kaf in His statement "كَأنْ" (ka'an, "as if") may be in the sense of a qualifier of the day, and it may be in the place of an adjective of the verbal noun, as if he said: "and the day We gather them a gathering as if they had not remained", and His statement ﴿as if they had not remained﴾ may be in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "يَحْشُرُهُمْ". The day was specified by mention because its hours and divisions are known and clear to all, so it is as if these people are certain of how little they remained, since every long period, once it has passed, is the same as a short one. As for His statement "يَتَعارَفُونَ", it is possible that it is parallel to His statement: ﴿And the day He gathers them⦆, as if He informed that on the day of gathering they will recognize one another, and this recognition is in the manner of mutual blaming and disgrace among them. It is possible that it is in the place of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "نَحْشُرُهُمْ", and the meaning of recognition is like the preceding one. It is possible that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "يَلْبَثُوا", and the recognition would be in this world, and the meaning of the verse would be: "and the day We gather them for the Resurrection, the knowledge among them and the means will be cut off, and their recognition in this world will be like an hour of the day that has no measure." Al-Tabari explained it in a manner close to this meaning. The Seven Readers and the majority of people read "نَحْشُرُهُمْ" with the nun, while al-A'mash, as is narrated from him, read "يَحْشُرُهُمْ" with the ya'.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who denied﴾ to the end of it, is a ruling upon the deniers with loss. In the wording there is severity toward those gathered, by showing what they are upon of deception regarding Allah the Exalted. This is on the basis that the speech is an informing from Allah, blessed and exalted is He. It was also said that it is from the speech of those gathered, in the manner of rebuking themselves.

The seeing in His statement "نُرِيَنَّكَ" (nurayannaka, "We show you") is sight, and the verb has been transitivized by the hamza, so it takes two objects: the first is the "كَ" (ka, "you"), and the second is "بَعْضَ" (ba'ḍa, "part of"). The reference in His statement ﴿part of what﴾ is to Allah's punishment upon them, such as Badr and others. The meaning of this verse is a warning of return to Allah the Exalted, that is: whether We show you their punishment or do not show it to you, they are in every state returning to Us, to reckoning and punishment. The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿For every nation there is a messenger; so when their messenger comes, judgment will be made between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say, "I possess not for myself any harm or benefit, except what Allah wills. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 50–53:

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿Say: Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day, what is there in it that the criminals would hasten?﴾ ﴿Is it only then, when it has befallen, that you will believe in it? Now? And you were, of it, those who used to hasten it?﴾ ﴿Then it will be said to those who wronged: Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?﴾ ﴿And they ask you, "Is it true?" Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it is true, and you cannot escape."﴾

The meaning: Say, O disbelievers who hasten the punishment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you﴾ at night, at the time of sleeping? It is said "bayyata al-qawm al-qawm" (they attacked the people at night) when they assault them at night with war or the like. Or "by day," when you have some defence against it or the strength to withstand it? Then what would you hasten of it, when you have no power against it? "Ma" is the subject (mubtada'), and "dha" is its predicate. It is also permissible that "madha" be a single word in the nominative position as the subject, with the sentence following it as its predicate. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) regarded this as weak and said: this is only permissible on the assumption of a hidden and omitted element in "yasta'jilu," as in the verse:

"............................. *** kulluhu lam aṣna'i"

and "Zaidun darabtu" (Zaid, I struck). He said: It is also permissible that "madha" be in the accusative position as the object of "yasta'jilu." The pronoun in "minhu" may refer back to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, or it may refer back to the punishment.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿Is it only then, when it has befallen﴾ and the rest of the verse, He has linked with "thumma" (then) the whole statement to what preceded it, and then placed the interrogative alif (alif al-taqrir, the alif of affirmation or confirmation) before the whole. The meaning of the verse: When the punishment falls and you witness it, you will believe in it at that time, but that will not benefit you. Rather, your answer now, when you used to hasten it while denying it, is ...

Talha ibn Musarrif recited "athamma" with a fatha on the thaa'. Al-Tabari said, regarding the words of the Exalted "thumma" with a damma on the thaa', that its meaning is "hunalika" (there, at that place), and he said: this "thumma" is not the one that comes to mean conjunction (ataf).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is sound if it is the well-known "thumma," but the consensus of the readers upon the wording of the revelation is as we have stated, and what al-Tabari claimed is not known. As for "al-an" (now), its origin according to some grammarians is "an," a past-tense verb, to which the alif and lam were attached in their usual manner, as in the line:

"............................. *** ***.......al-himaru al-yujaddu'"

It did not become fully definite by this, but it is a word that contains the meaning of the definite article, and for that reason it is built on fatha, because it includes the meaning of a particle and because it occupies the place of the indefinite, since its meaning is "this time." Al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and the majority read "a-l-an" with a long vowel and as an interrogative, in the manner of reproach, and likewise "a-l-an wa-qad 'asayta" (Now? And you had already disobeyed). Talha and al-A'raj read it as an interrogative without the long vowel.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then it will be said to those who wronged﴾ and the rest of the verse, this is the greatest threat of eternal abiding for the people of the most specific wrongdoing, which is the wrong of disbelief, not the wrong of sin. His words ﴿Are you recompensed?﴾ are a rebuke and a reproach. This verse states explicitly that the recompense in the Hereafter is according to the earning of the servant.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And they ask you﴾, the meaning is "yastakhbirunaka" (they ask you for information). On this understanding it takes two objects: the first is the kaf (you), and the second is the subject and predicate (the clause "is it true?"). It was also said that it means "yasta'limunaka" (they seek knowledge from you), and on this understanding it requires three objects: the first is the kaf, and the subject and predicate fill the place of the two objects.

As for ﴿Is it true?﴾, it was said that the reference is to the Law and the Qur'an, and it was said that it refers to the threat, which is the more apparent view. Al-A'mash read "al-haqqu huwa" with a long vowel and with the definite article. His words "i" (yes) are a word that precedes an oath, and it means "na'am" (yes). After it comes the particle of oath, though it may not come. You say "i wa-rabbi" and "i rabbi" (Yes, by my Lord). "Mu'jizin" means "mufiltin" (those who escape). The original form of this verb is the transitive form of "'ajaza," but the omission of the object became so common in it that the Arabs said "a'jaza fulanun" (so-and-so escaped) when he went off in the land and could not be overtaken.

After it comes the particle of oath, though it may not come. You say "i wa-rabbi" and "i rabbi" (Yes, by my Lord). "Mu'jizin" means "mufiltin" (those who escape). The original form of this verb is the transitive form of "'ajaza," but the omission of the object became so common in it that the Arabs said "a'jaza fulanun" (so-and-so escaped) when he went off in the land and could not be overtaken.

(p-492) The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿Had every soul that did wrong possessed all that is on the earth, it would surely offer it as ransom. And they will hide their regret when they see the punishment. And judgment will be passed between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Surely, the promise of Allah is true, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

This is information for the disbelievers, in the context of informing them that this promise is true. It also comes with the meaning "they displayed," in which case it derives from "asarir al-wajh" (the lines of the face). Al-Tabari said: the meaning is that the leaders of these disbelievers concealed the regret from their followers and their subordinates.

Rather, it is general to all of them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The linking of the two verses in this way is plausible but distant, and this is not among the eloquent aims. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 57–58:

The words of the Most High:

﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy—in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾

This is a verse addressed to the whole world. The mawʿiẓa (admonition) is the Qur'an, because wa'ẓ (admonition) is only by speech that commands what is good, restrains, softens the heart, threatens and promises, and this is the description of the Mighty Book. His words ﴿from your Lord﴾ mean: Muhammad ﷺ did not fabricate it, nor did anyone else; rather it is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for ﴿for what is in the breasts﴾, it means ignorance and obstinacy in reflecting upon the signs of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and similar things that repel faith. He made it an admonition according to all people, and made it guidance and mercy only for the believers. This is an interpretation whose meaning is sound; when it is pondered, its aspect becomes clear.

As for His, glorified be He, words ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy"﴾, the bāʾ (the preposition "in") is connected to an omitted verb that is dispensed with in mention and is indicated by His words ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾. Some of those who interpreted it, namely Hilal ibn Yasaf, Qatada, al-Hasan, and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them, said: the bounty (fadl) is Islam, and the mercy (raḥma) is the Qur'an. Abu Saʿid al-Khudri said: the bounty is the Qur'an, and the mercy is that He made them among its people. Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Dahhak said: the bounty is the Qur'an, and the mercy is Islam. A group said: the bounty is Muhammad ﷺ, and the mercy is the Qur'an.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view there is no basis for any of this specification, unless some of it is traced back to the Prophet ﷺ. What the wording requires, and what necessarily follows from it, is that the bounty is Allah's guidance to His religion and His granting success in following His law, and the mercy is His pardon and dwelling in His Garden, which He made a reward for adhering to Islam and believing in it. The meaning of the verse is: Say, O Muhammad, to all people: "In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy, let joy fall upon you, not upon the affairs of this world and what it gathers of its debris." So the believers are told: "Then rejoice," and they are already engaged in the cause and reason of joy, and attaining the bounty of Allah while awaiting His mercy. And the disbelievers are told: "In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy, then rejoice," in the sense of: if it were to befall you, or if you were made happy by being guided to attaining that.

Abu Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, and al-Hasan—according to what Harun claimed—and it was also related from the Prophet ﷺ, read ﴿فَلْتَفْرَحُوا (falyafraḥū)﴾ and ﴿تَجْمَعُونَ (tajmaʿūn)﴾ with the letter tāʾ in both, in the form of direct address. This is the reading of a large group of the early generations (salaf), though most of them differ on it. The Seven Readers other than Ibn ʿAmir, the people of Madina, al-Aʿraj, Mujahid, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Qatada, Talha, and al-Aʿmash read both with the letter yāʾ, in the form of third-person reference. It was related from al-Hasan with tāʾ at the beginning in both. Abu al-Tayyah, Abu Jaʿfar, Qatada—according to a difference reported from them—and Ibn ʿAmir read with yāʾ in the first and tāʾ in the last. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and a group of the early generations read with yāʾ in both the first and the last, and it was related from the Prophet ﷺ; it was also related from Abu al-Tayyah. When you reflect upon the aspects of these readings, they turn out to be in line with the eloquent usage of the Arabic language, and for this reason the disagreement among every reciter is abundant. In the Codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb the reading is ﴿فَبِذَلِكَ فافْرَحُوا (fabidhālika fa-fraḥū)﴾. As for whoever reads ﴿فَلْتَفْرَحُوا (falyafraḥū)﴾, placing the lām in the imperative addressed to the second person, this is according to a rare dialect, which Abu ʿAli related in al-Hujja. Abu Hatim and others said: the original rule for every imperative is to introduce the lām when the command is by a particle; likewise, the imperative for an absent party is with lām. Abu al-Fath said: however, the Arabs rejected introducing the lām into the imperative addressed to the second person because of its frequent recurrence. Abu al-Tayyah and al-Hasan read ﴿فَلْتَفْرَحُوا﴾ with a kasra on the lām.

If it is asked: how did Allah command joy in this verse, when its blame has come in His words ﴿Indeed, he is a boastful exultant﴾ [Hud: 10], and in His words ﴿Do not exult; indeed, Allah does not love the exultant﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]? It is said: joy, when it occurs restricted to good, is not blameworthy, and so it is in this verse. When it occurs restricted to evil, or unrestricted, blame attaches to it, since it is not among the acts of the Hereafter; rather, a person should be predominantly overcome by sorrow over his sin and fear of his Lord. His words ﴿better than what they accumulate﴾ mean: better than the wealth of this world and its perishing debris, which harms in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 59–60:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: "Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision, and you have made from it the forbidden and the lawful?" Say: "Has God permitted you, or do you fabricate against God?"﴾ ﴿And what will be the opinion of those who fabricate against God the lie on the Day of Resurrection? Indeed, God is Bountiful to mankind, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾

This address is to the disbelieving Arabs who made the baḥāʾir (she-camels whose ears were slit and who were released), the sawāʾib (animals released to roam freely), the naṣīb (a portion set aside) from the tilth and the livestock, and other things that God had not permitted, and they only invented them by their own command. His saying, Most High: ﴿sent down﴾ is a word in which there is a figurative usage (tajawwuz), and the sending down of provision is either within the sending down of rain with its produce, or the descent of the command concerning it, which is the appearance of the effect in the created thing brought forth from it. Then God commanded His Prophet to make them stand on one of the two divisions, and they could not claim God's permission in that, so nothing remained but that they had fabricated it. This verse is similar to His saying, Most High: ﴿Say: "Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He brought forth for His servants?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 32]. Al-Tabari mentioned this from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father.

His saying, Most High: ﴿And what will be the opinion of those who fabricate against God﴾ is a verse of warning. Since it was established against them, through the division in the preceding verse, that they are fabricators against God, in this verse He magnified the gravity of fabrication; that is, their opinion is in the utmost baseness according to the evil of their deeds. Then He followed it with affirming the bounty upon mankind in granting them respite despite their fabrication and disobedience; respite is a call to repentance and turning back. Then He added a mention of those who do not recognize the true worth of respite, do not thank for it, and do not hasten toward it, by way of censure of them. And the verse after this encompasses all of God's bounty and all of the creatures' shortcoming in giving thanks to Him, there is no lord other than Him.

[p. 496]

The words of the Most High: ﴿You are not engaged in any affair, nor do you recite any part of the Qur'an, nor do you do any deed, but We are witnesses over you when you are deeply engaged in it. Not an atom's weight in the earth or in the heaven escapes your Lord, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ ﴿Those who believed and used to be mindful of Allah.﴾

The purpose of the verse is to describe Allah's encompassing knowledge of everything. The meaning of the wording is: "You, O Muhammad, and others besides you, are not engaged in any affair among all affairs." ﴿Nor do you recite any part of it﴾: the pronoun refers to "affair," meaning "in it and because of it, any part of the Qur'an." It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the whole Qur'an, and then the statement generalizes with His words ﴿nor do you do any deed﴾. In His words ﴿but We are witnesses over you﴾ there is a warning and an alert. ﴿Tufidun﴾ (you are deeply engaged): you take up and rise to it with earnestness. It is said: "afada al-rajulu" (the man plunged) in his journey and in his speech, and from it comes "al-ifada" (the outpouring) in the Hajj, and "mufid al-qidah" (the one who casts the arrows). It is possible that "fada" is made transitive by the hamza.

"Ya'zub" means: it goes away until it becomes hidden, to the extent that they call the distant one "a'zib." From it is the verse of the poet:

*Strays that have not heard the barking of a dwelling place,*
*nor seen a fire kindled over a full year of hardship.*

It was also said of one who is absent from his family that he is "a'zib," until they said it of one who has no wife. In the biographies it is reported that the house of Sa'd ibn Khaythamah was called "the house of the bachelors." The majority of the seven readers and the people read "ya'zub" with a *damma* on the *zay*. Al-Kisa'i alone among them read "ya'zib" with a *kasra* on it, and this is the reading of Ibn Thabbat, al-A'mash and Talhah ibn Musarrif. Abu Hatim said: reading with *damma* and with *kasra* are both dialectal variants.

*Al-mithqal* means the weight. It is a noun, not an adjective, like *mi'tar* and *midrab*. *Al-dharr* means the smallest ants. Allah made it an example, since among animals that feed and reproduce, of well-known kind and place, nothing is smaller than it.

The majority of the people and most of the seven readers read ﴿wa la asghara﴾ and ﴿wa la akbara﴾ with a *fatha* on the *ra'*, in coordination with *dharrah* in a position of genitive, but the impossibility of inflection (*imtina' al-sarf*) prevented its visible marking. Hamzah alone read ﴿wa la asghara﴾ and ﴿wa la akbaru﴾ in coordination with the position of His words *mithqal*, because the sense is: "and nothing escapes your Lord, the weight of an atom."

*Al-Kitab al-Mubin* (the Clear Book) is the Preserved Tablet, as some of the exegetes said. It is possible that it means the recording of the scribes, and the purpose would be the mention of the deeds mentioned before. The placement of "the smaller" first in the order follows their saying "al-qamarayn" (the two moons) and "al-'umarayn" (the two 'Umars), and from it is His statement: ﴿It leaves nothing small or great unrecorded﴾ (18:49). The purpose of all this is to alert to the lesser, and that if the intended ruling applies to the lesser, it is all the more applicable to the greater.

*Ala* is an opening and alerting particle. The friends of Allah (*awliya' Allah*) are the believers who have shown loyalty to Him through obedience and worship. The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that whoever believes and is mindful is included among the friends of Allah, and this is what the Shari'ah requires regarding the *wali* (friend of Allah). We have given this caution only out of fear of some who are literalist in their view of the *wali* and of some atheists concerning the *wali*. And in Sahih Muslim, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Nothing remains of the good tidings except the righteous dream." And Umm Kurz al-Ka'biyyah narrated from him that he said: "Prophethood has departed, and the good tidings remain." Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the good news in this world is what the believer is given tidings of at his death while he is still alive, at the moment of witnessing.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that the good news of this world is what is in the Qur'an of verses bearing good tidings, and this is strengthened by His saying in this verse: ﴿There is no alteration in the words of Allah.﴾ Yet all of that is opposed by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "It is the dream," unless we say that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave an example of the good news, and it encompasses all people. His saying ﴿There is no alteration in the words of Allah﴾ means: there is no breaking of His promises and no reversal of His command.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

'Abdullah ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) understood this in a different manner, and took the alteration that is negated to be in the wording. It was reported that al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf delivered a sermon and prolonged it until he said: "Indeed 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr has altered the Book of Allah." 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar said to him: "You are not able to do that, neither you nor Ibn al-Zubayr: ﴿There is no alteration in the words of Allah.﴾" al-Hajjaj said to him: "You have been given (p-500) knowledge." When he left him in private, he remained silent about him. This view was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas outside of the dispute with al-Hajjaj; al-Bukhari mentioned it. His saying ﴿That is the great triumph﴾ is a reference to the bliss through which the good tidings occurred.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And let not...﴾ the verse. This is a verse of consolation for Muhammad (ﷺ), and the meaning is: Let not their speech grieve you, O Muhammad, nor worry you, that is, the speech of the disbelievers of Quraysh. The word "speech" encompasses their denial, their mockery, their deception, and other things.

Then he began with the statement that all might belongs to Allah, that is: they are unable to do anything, and they cannot harm you except by what Allah wills, and He is capable of punishing them, nothing overpowers Him. So in the verse there is a warning for them. The "inna" is kasra-vowelled at the beginning and has no connection to the preceding speech. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is not permissible to open the "inna" in this position, and that would be disbelief.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying "and that would be disbelief" is an exaggeration, and it seems that this would be construed as: because all might belongs to Allah. His saying ﴿He is the All-Hearing﴾, that is, of everything they say, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what is in their souls of that; and within these attributes is a threat. Then he opened with His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾, that is, by ownership and encompassing. He gave precedence to "man" (those who reason) in His saying "man," since to Him belongs the dominion of all that is in them and of whoever is in them. Since the expression came with "má," this is a case of giving precedence to the majority, for the greater number of created things does not reason; so "man" applies to both categories together, and "má" is likewise. It is not applied to what reasons when stripped of attributes and states. Do you not see that if I mention to you a statement in a matter and you wish to ask about its speaker, is it permissible in the speech of the Arabs to say: "What is the speaker of this statement?" This is what one who understands the speech of the Arabs holds to. His saying ﴿And what do they follow﴾ may be such that "má" is interrogative, meaning confirmation and drawing the addressee's attention, and "yad'ūna" operates on "shuraka'" (partners). It may also be negating, with "yattabi'u" operating on "shuraka'" in the sense that they do not truly follow partners; the object of "yad'ūna" would then be omitted, and in my view this aspect involves strain. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "tad'ūna" with the ta', and this reading is not well-founded. His saying "in" is negating, and "yakhruṣūna" means: they conjecture and guess, not speaking by analogy or reflection. One group read "wa-lā yuḥzinka" from aḥzana, and another group read "wa-lā yaḥzunka" from ḥazana.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 67–70:

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

﴿It is He who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight. Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen.﴾ ﴿They said, "Allah has taken a son." Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. You have no authority for this. Do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, those who invent falsehood against Allah will not succeed."﴾ ﴿[They have] a brief enjoyment in this world; then to Us is their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾

When He mentioned the greatness of Allah, blessed and exalted, in the preceding verse, He followed that in this verse with a reminder of His acts, to make clear the greatness that was affirmed before. His saying ﴿that you may rest therein﴾ indicates that the day is for movement and activity, and so it is in existence, since movement at night is impossible due to the absence of light. His saying ﴿and the day giving sight﴾ is a metaphor, because the day does not see; rather it is the time (zarf) for seeing. This usage exists in the speech of the Arabs, since the intended meaning is understood. Among that is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:(p-502)

؎ "You blamed us, O Umm Ghaylan, during the night journey, and you slept, while the night of the camels is not sleeping."

This is not of the type of attribution (nasab) such as ʿīshatin rāḍiyah (a pleasing life) and the like. Rather, it is like the saying of the poet:

؎ "As for the day, it is in shackles and chain, and the night is in the belly of a hollowed-out piece of teak wood."

So he made the night and the day into these two states, and he intends only that he is in them in such a way. This verse belongs to a prisoner who used to spend the night in the wooden stocks of the prison. It is also recited as "Amma al-nahar" with the accusative. In these words there is concision and reliance on the listener's mind, because the lesson lies in the fact that the night is dark, in which one rests, and the day is bright, in which one acts. One side is mentioned, and the other side from the other aspect, and what is mentioned indicates what is left out. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and cry﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171]. His saying ﴿they hear﴾ means: they comprehend (ya'un). The pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ refers to the Arab disbelievers, and this is the saying of a group among them: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." The verse nonetheless covers everyone who says something similar to this statement, such as the Christians and whoever among the disbelievers may hold that belief. "Subhanahu" is a verbal noun whose meaning is: exalting Him and declaring Him free of that. The Prophet ﷺ explained it with this meaning. His saying ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient﴾ is a description in absolute terms, meaning He is not in need of anything from any aspect, and a son is a part of what He is free from. The truth is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿You are the poor toward Allah﴾ [Fatir: 15]. His saying ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ refers to ownership, encompassment and creation. "In" is negative, and "sultan" means proof (hujjah); its meaning is likewise wherever it recurs in the Qur'an. Then He stopped them, rebuking them, with His saying: ﴿Do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ (p-503)

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Indeed, those who invent falsehood against Allah"﴾, the verse is a warning to them that they will not attain their aim and will not remain in blessing, since this is the state of one who proceeds to punishment, even if he is granted some comfort in his worldly life. His saying "matāʿ" (enjoyment) is in the nominative as the predicate of an inchoative, meaning: that is an enjoyment; or it is in the inchoative with the implied sense: for them is an enjoyment. His saying ﴿then to Us is their return﴾ to the end of the verse is a true warning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 71:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And recite to them the story of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of Allah is burdensome to you, then in Allah I have put my trust. So resolve upon your affair, and (gather) your associates, then let your affair not be hidden from you (lit. a distress upon you). Then carry it out against me and do not give me respite."﴾

The word "Noah" has already been discussed in "al-A'raf". Al-maqam (المقام) is the man's standing up for a speech, a sermon or the like. Al-muqam, with a dammah on the mim, is his residing in a place or a city. It is not read here with a dammah on the mim. Tadhkir (تذكير) is his admonishing and warning. The meaning is: O my people, if you consider my condition and my calling you to Allah to be insignificant, then I do not care about you, because I rely upon Allah the Exalted; so do whatever you are able to do.

The Seven Readers, and the majority of people, along with al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa, read "fa-ajmi'u" (فَأجْمِعُوا), from ajma'a al-rajulu 'ala shay'in (أجْمَعَ الرَجُلُ عَلى شَيْءٍ), meaning to resolve firmly upon something. From this is the saying of the poet:

"... Shall I go out one day while my resolve is firm?"

And from it the saying of another:

"They resolved their affair by night, and when they arose in the morning, a clamour came upon them."

And from it the hadith: "... as long as he has not resolved to stay (mukthan)." And from it the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"He mentioned the watering there, and so resolved, out of longing, while his time came to follow (it)."

Nafi' (as transmitted from him by al-Asma'i), and it is the reading of al-A'raj, Ibn Abi Raja', 'Asim al-Jahdari, al-Zuhri and al-A'mash, read "fa-jma'u" (فاجْمَعُوا) with a fathah on the mim, from jama'a, meaning to join one thing to another. By "amrakum" he means your power and your life. This reading is supported by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew and gathered his schemes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 60]. All of these put "al-shuraka'" (the associates) in the accusative. The accusative of His saying "shuraka'akum" may be understood as coordinated with His saying "amrakum"; this is on the reading "fa-jma'u" with a wasl (connected) alif. As for the one who reads "fa-ajmi'u" with a cut alif, the accusative of "al-shuraka'" is by a hidden verb, as if he said: "and call upon your associates", so it is from the same type as the saying of the poet:

"A drinker of milk, and dates, and aqit (dried curd)."

And like the saying of another:

"And I saw your husband in battle, girded with a sword and a spear."

And like the saying of another:

"I fed her hay and cold water, until her two eyes streamed with tears."

In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "fa-ajmi'u amrakum wad'u shuraka'akum" (So resolve upon your affair and call upon your associates). Abu 'Ali said: "al-shuraka'" may also be in the accusative by the waw of "ma'a" (with), as they said: "The mail-carrier came with the tayalisa" (the shawl-wearers). Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa, Salam, Ya'qub, and Abu 'Amr, as transmitted from him, read "wa-shurakauukum" (وَشُرَكاؤُكُمْ) with the nominative, coordinated with the pronoun in "fa-ajmi'u". It was coordinated with the pronoun before it was emphasized, because the kaf and mim in "amrakum" stand in the place of "antum" (you), which emphasizes the pronoun, and also because of the length of the speech. This phrasing is better than letting the speech become long without a pronoun. It is also permissible for it to be nominative by the inchoative, with the predicate understood, its estimate being: "and their associates, let them then resolve". A group read "wa-shuraka'ikum" (وَشُرَكائِكُمْ) with the genitive, coordinated with the pronoun in His saying ﴿amrakum﴾, the estimate being "and the affair of your associates". It is like the saying of the poet:

"Is every man you think a man, and a fire that blazes at night a fire?"

That is: and every fire. What is meant by "al-shuraka'" in this verse is the rivals besides Allah, and He attributed them to them, since they make them associates by their own claim.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then let not your affair be a distress upon you﴾, that is, obscure and confusing. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ regarding the crescent: "If it is hidden from you (fa-in ghumma 'alaykum)," and from it the saying of the rajiz:

"Rather, had you witnessed the people when they were enveloped in a distress, unless it is relieved, they would be distressed."

His saying: ﴿Then carry it out against me﴾ means: execute your decision toward me. Al-Suddi ibn Ya'nam read "thumma afduu" (ثُمَّ أفْضُوا) with a fa' and a cut alif, meaning: hasten. It is derived from the open wide land (al-ard al-fada'), that is: proceed toward me with your scheme and come out with me and against me into a wide space. His saying: ﴿and do not give me respite﴾, that is: do not delay me. Al-nazrah (النَظِرَةُ) is delay.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 72–73:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And if you turn away, then I have not asked you for any wage. My wage is only from Allah, and I have been commanded to be among those who submit.﴾ ﴿But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So see how was the end of those who were warned.﴾

The meaning: If you do not turn toward my call, and disbelieve in it, and turn away from it. The root of tawallī (turning away) is with the body, and it is used for turning away from meanings. He says: I have not asked you for a wage for this, nor for money, so that a cutting off from you would befall me, or a shortcoming in my purpose; rather my wage is upon the One who sent me. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr, in one of the transmissions from him, read "ajrī" with a sukūn on the yā'. Al-A'raj, Talha ibn Musarrif, 'Isa, and Abu 'Amr read "ajriya" with a fatḥah on the yā'. Abu Ḥatim said: "They are two dialects, and the recitation with sukūn is the one used throughout the Qur'an." Then he informed them that Allah had commanded him to submit (Islam) and to the upright religion (dīn ḥanīf), which is the affirmation of Allah's oneness, acting in obedience to Him, and preparing for meeting Him.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿But they denied him﴾ and the verse: it is an report from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, about the condition of the people of Noah who denied him (p-507). Within this report is a warning to the disbelievers concerning Muhammad ﷺ and a presenting of an example for them, meaning: you are in the same state of denial as these, so you will be in their state of retribution and punishment. "Al-Fulk" is the ship. The exegetes and the people of narrations are unanimous that the ship of Noah was one ship. The word "al-fulk" is the same in singular and plural form, and it is not meant for the singular only; the explanation of this has already passed in "al-A'raf." "Khala'if" is the plural of khalifah. His saying "fa-nzur" (so see) is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and all creation shares with him in its meaning. In this verse it is stated that He drowned all who denied the signs of Allah which Noah, peace be upon him, brought, and it also implies that he warned them, so they were "those who were warned." If they were all the people of the earth, as some people have said, then Noah and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both, would be equal in being sent to the people of the earth, and this is refuted by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I have been given five things which no one before me was given" (the hadith). By this reasoning it becomes more probable that the mission of Noah, peace be upon him, and the drowning were only for the people of a region, not for all the people of the earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 72–73:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And if you turn away, then I have not asked you for any wage. My wage is only from Allah, and I have been commanded to be among those who submit.﴾ ﴿But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So see how was the end of those who were warned.﴾

The meaning: If you do not turn toward my call, and disbelieve in it, and turn away from it. The root of tawallī (turning away) is with the body, and it is used for turning away from meanings. He says: I have not asked you for a wage for this, nor for money, so that a cutting off from you would befall me, or a shortcoming in my purpose; rather my wage is upon the One who sent me. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 74–75:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs, but they were not to believe in what they had denied before. Thus We seal the hearts of the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Then after them We sent Musa and Harun to Fir'awn and his chiefs with Our signs, but they were arrogant and were a criminal people.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "min ba'dihi" (after him) refers to Nuh (peace be upon him), and the pronoun in "qawmihim" (their peoples) refers to the messengers. The meaning of all these verses is to set forth an example for the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ): that is, what befell these people will befall you. "Al-bayyinat" means the miracles and the clear proofs. The pronoun in His saying "kanu" (they were) and in "liyu'minu" (to believe) refers to the people of the messengers, and the pronoun in "kanu" refers to the people of Nuh (peace be upon him). This is the view of some of the interpreters. Others said: rather, all three pronouns refer to the people of the messengers, in the sense that whenever a messenger came, they rushed to deny their messenger, then they persisted in disbelief and continued in it, so they were not to believe in what their denial had preceded. Yahya ibn Salam said: "min qabl" means: before the punishment.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is remote. In my opinion the wording admits another meaning, namely that "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle, and the meaning is: they denied their messengers, so their punishment from Allah was that they were not to believe, because of their denial, before it, that is, from its cause and from its recompense. This interpretation is supported by His saying: ﴿Thus We seal﴾. Some scholars said: the punishment for denial is the sealing upon the hearts. The majority of readers recited "natba'u" (We seal) with the nun, and al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl recited "yatba'u" with the ya. His saying "kadhalika" (thus) means: this is Our action toward these people; then He began: ﴿Thus We seal﴾, that is, like this action of Ours. ﴿Al-mu'tadin﴾ (the transgressors) are those who exceeded their bounds and committed what is not permitted to them, and here it is in disbelief.

The pronoun in "ba'dihim" (after them) refers to the messengers, and the pronoun in "wa-mala'ihi" (and his chiefs) refers to Fir'awn. Al-mala' (the chiefs) means the group of a tribe or the people of a city; then the term is applied to the nobles and notables of the tribe or city, "mala'", meaning they stand in the place of the group. On this basis it is used in the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) saying about the Quraysh at Badr: "Those are the mala'." Likewise it is used in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the chiefs are conferring about you﴾ [al-Qasas: 20]. As for this verse, it is general, because the mission of Musa and Harun was to Fir'awn and all his people, both noble and common. Their mention and what they were sent with has already passed in ﴿Al-Mim-Sad﴾ [al-A'raf: 1]. "Al-ayat" means the proofs, the miracles and what has their meaning. His saying ﴿fa-istakbaru﴾ (but they were arrogant) means: they magnified themselves and disbelieved in them. "Mujrimin" means: they commit what Allah has not permitted, and they dare in that toward a grave peril.

(p-509) His words, Mighty and Majestic be He:

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Indeed, this is clear magic."﴾ ﴿Moses said, "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, 'Is this magic?' And magicians do not succeed."﴾ ﴿They said, "Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon, and that you two may have grandeur (al-kibriya') in the land? We are not going to believe you two."﴾

By "the truth" (al-haqq) He means the two signs, the staff and the hand. This is shown by their saying in their presence, "This is magic," and they said that only in their presence, and they did not undertake anything except opposing the staff, which is the miracle of Moses, peace be upon him, the one in which the opponent's inability became manifest. The majority of readers recited "la-sihrun mubin" (indeed, clear magic), while Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-A'mash recited "la-sahirun mubin" (indeed, a clear magician).

Then the interpreters differed regarding His words, "Is this magic?" One group said: it is a report from Moses about them, meaning that their statement was, "Is this magic?" Then it was disputed about the meaning of the statement of the people of Pharaoh, "Is this magic?" Some of them said: every inquirer who is ignorant of the matter says it, so he asks about it.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is weakened by what Allah mentioned before concerning them, that they were resolute that it is magic, by their saying: "Indeed, this is clear magic." Others said: rather, they said that in the sense of magnifying the magic which they saw, by their claim, just as you say to a horse which you see running well, "Is this a horse?" meaning in wonder at it and amazement, while you know that it is a horse. Another group besides these two said: that is not a report from Moses about them; rather, the statement that He reported from them is implied, its estimated form being: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, 'Is it magic?'"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Or something similar to this estimation. Then he begins to confront them with His words, "Is this magic?" as a rebuke. Then He informed them about Allah, Exalted, that magicians do not succeed and do not attain their aim. A similar omitted estimation according to this interpretation exists in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"So when they wrapped the night, or when they raised toward him from the cover of their ears, and he was inclining..."

He means: or when they approached that. And from it is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, to distress your faces﴾ [al-Isra: 7], meaning: We sent them so that they would distress. Similar to this is common and widespread.

As for His words, Exalted, "They said, 'Have you come to us...'" the verse means: the people of Pharaoh said to Moses, "Have you come to us to turn us aside, twist us, and return us from the religion of our fathers?" It is said, "lafata al-rajul 'an al-akhar" when he turned him away, and from it their saying "iltafata," for it is an iftial from "lafta 'unuqahu" (he twisted his neck). And from it is the saying of Ru'bah:

"Twisting and bending, equal in twisting..."

The Seven Readers, except Abu 'Amr, for whom there is a difference reported, recited "wa-takuna" with the taa' from above, and this is the recitation of the majority of people. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, according to what Kharija and Isma'il reported, recited "wa-yakuna" with the ya' from below; it is also reported from Abu 'Amr and from 'Asim, and it is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud. "Al-kibriya'" is an intensive verbal noun from "al-kibr" (pride), and what is meant by it in this place is kingship; Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and most of the interpreters said the same, because it is the greatest of worldly pride. From it is the saying of the poet:

"A lordship, not shameful, which is not oppressive to its owner, nor is there grandeur (kibriya')..."

(p-511) As for His words, "bi-mu'minin" (believers), it means: "believing in you" in the sense of confirming (musaddiqin).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 79–82:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And Pharaoh said: "Bring me every learned magician."﴾ ﴿So when the magicians came, Moses said to them: "Throw down what you are going to throw."﴾ ﴿So when they had thrown, Moses said: "What you have brought is magic. Indeed, Allah will render it void. Indeed, Allah does not set right the work of the corrupters."﴾ ﴿And Allah will establish the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it.﴾

He informs that Pharaoh said to his servants and agents: "Bring me every magician." This is the reading of the majority of people. Talha ibn Musarrif, Yahya ibn Wathhab and Isa read "bi-kulli sahhar" (every great magician), for emphasis. Abu Hatim said: "We do not read sahhar except in Surat ash-Shu'ara'." It is narrated that they brought him magicians from al-Farama and other lands of Egypt, as has been mentioned earlier in other than this verse. When the magicians arrived, prepared to oppose him, they gave Moses the choice, as has been mentioned in other than this verse. He then said to them, by the command of Allah: ﴿Throw down what you are going to throw.﴾

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they had thrown﴾ and the rest of the verse, the meaning is: when they threw their ropes and their staffs and created an illusion with them, and they assumed that they had prevailed, Moses said this statement to them. The Seven Readers, except Abu 'Amr, read ﴿bihi as-sihr﴾, which is the reading of the majority of people. Abu 'Amr, Mujahid and his companions, and Ibn al-Qa'qa' read "bihi aas-sihr" with an interrogative alif before "as-sihr," elongated. As for the one who reads "as-sihr" without an interrogative alif before it, then "ma" is in the nominative position as the subject of the nominal sentence, meaning "that which" (alladhi), and its relative clause is His saying ﴿you have brought﴾, the returning pronoun being the pronoun in "bihi," and its predicate is "as-sihr." This reading and interpretation are supported by the fact that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "What you have brought is magic (ma ji'tum bihi sihrun)," and likewise al-A'mash recited it, and it is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "What you have brought is magic (ma ataytum bihi sihrun)." The definiteness here in "as-sihr" is more fitting, because it was previously mentioned indefinitely in their saying: "Indeed, this is surely magic (inna hadha lasihrun)," so it comes here with the definite article of prior reference, just as one says at the beginning of a letter: "Peace be upon you," and at its end: "And peace be upon you."

It is also permissible that "ma" be an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject, with "ji'tum bihi" as the predicate, and "as-sihr" the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being: "It is the magic; indeed Allah will render it void." The purpose of this interrogation is affirmation and rebuke. It is also permissible that "ma" be in the accusative position, meaning "what thing you have brought," with "as-sihr" in the nominative as the predicate of the subject; the sense of the sentence being: "What thing you have brought, it is the magic; indeed Allah will render it void."

As for the one who reads with the interrogative alif and the elongation before "as-sihr," then "ma" is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject, and "ji'tum bihi" is the predicate, and this is in the manner of affirmation. His saying "as-sihr" is likewise an interrogative, and it is a substitute (badal) for the first interrogative. It is also permissible that "ma" be in the accusative position governed by an implied verb whose explanation is in His saying ﴿you have brought﴾, its estimate being: "What thing you have brought, the magic?" His saying ﴿indeed Allah will render it void﴾ is an affirmation of a promise from Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will establish the truth﴾ and the rest of the verse, it may be that it is part of Moses's speech, peace be upon him, and it may be that it is a report from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. That all of this is part of Moses's speech, peace be upon him, is closer to the truth, and this is what al-Tabari mentioned. As for His saying ﴿by His words﴾, its meaning is: by His earlier, eternal words concerning the promise of that. Ibn Salam said: ﴿by His words﴾ means by His saying: ﴿Fear not﴾ [Ta-Ha: 68]. The meaning of ﴿even if the criminals dislike it﴾ is: even if the criminals dislike it. The mujrim (criminal) is the one who commits sin, the one who engages in peril.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 79–82:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And Pharaoh said: "Bring me every learned magician."﴾ ﴿So when the magicians came, Moses said to them: "Throw down what you are going to throw."﴾ ﴿So when they had thrown, Moses said: "What you have brought is magic. Indeed, Allah will render it void. Indeed, Allah does not set right the work of the corrupters."﴾ ﴿And Allah will establish the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it.﴾

He informs that Pharaoh said to his servants and agents: "Bring me every magician." This is the reading of the majority of people. Talha ibn Musarrif, Yahya ibn Wathhab and Isa read "bi-kulli sahhar" (every great magician), for emphasis. Abu Hatim said: "We do not read sahhar except in Surat ash-Shu'ara'." It is narrated that they brought him magicians from al-Farama and other lands of Egypt, as has been mentioned earlier in other than this verse. When the magicians arrived, prepared to oppose him, they gave Moses the choice, as has been mentioned in other than this verse. He then said to them, by the command of Allah: ﴿Throw down what you are going to throw.﴾

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they had thrown﴾ and the rest of the verse, the meaning is: when they threw their ropes and their staffs and created an illusion with them, and they assumed that they had prevailed, Moses said this statement to them. The Seven Readers, except Abu 'Amr, read ﴿bihi as-sihr﴾, which is the reading of the majority of people. Abu 'Amr, Mujahid and his companions, and Ibn al-Qa'qa' read "bihi aas-sihr" with an interrogative alif before "as-sihr," elongated. As for the one who reads "as-sihr" without an interrogative alif before it, then "ma" is in the nominative position as the subject of the nominal sentence, meaning "that which" (alladhi), and its relative clause is His saying ﴿you have brought﴾, the returning pronoun being the pronoun in "bihi," and its predicate is "as-sihr." This reading and interpretation are supported by the fact that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "What you have brought is magic (ma ji'tum bihi sihrun)," and likewise al-A'mash recited it, and it is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "What you have brought is magic (ma ataytum bihi sihrun)." The definiteness here in "as-sihr" is more fitting, because it was previously mentioned indefinitely in their saying: "Indeed, this is surely magic (inna hadha lasihrun)," so it comes here with the definite article of prior reference, just as one says at the beginning of a letter: "Peace be upon you," and at its end: "And peace be upon you."

It is also permissible that "ma" be an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject, with "ji'tum bihi" as the predicate, and "as-sihr" the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being: "It is the magic; indeed Allah will render it void." The purpose of this interrogation is affirmation and rebuke. It is also permissible that "ma" be in the accusative position, meaning "what thing you have brought," with "as-sihr" in the nominative as the predicate of the subject; the sense of the sentence being: "What thing you have brought, it is the magic; indeed Allah will render it void."

As for the one who reads with the interrogative alif and the elongation before "as-sihr," then "ma" is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject, and "ji'tum bihi" is the predicate, and this is in the manner of affirmation. His saying "as-sihr" is likewise an interrogative, and it is a substitute (badal) for the first interrogative. It is also permissible that "ma" be in the accusative position governed by an implied verb whose explanation is in His saying ﴿you have brought﴾, its estimate being: "What thing you have brought, the magic?" His saying ﴿indeed Allah will render it void﴾ is an affirmation of a promise from Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will establish the truth﴾ and the rest of the verse, it may be that it is part of Moses's speech, peace be upon him, and it may be that it is a report from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. That all of this is part of Moses's speech, peace be upon him, is closer to the truth, and this is what al-Tabari mentioned. As for His saying ﴿by His words﴾, its meaning is: by His earlier, eternal words concerning the promise of that. Ibn Salam said: ﴿by His words﴾ means by His saying: ﴿Fear not﴾ [Ta-Ha: 68]. The meaning of ﴿even if the criminals dislike it﴾ is: even if the criminals dislike it. The mujrim (criminal) is the one who commits sin, the one who engages in peril.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 10, verses 83–86:**

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿But none believed in Moses except some of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their leaders, that he would persecute them. Indeed, Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the extravagant.﴾ ﴿And Moses said, "O my people, if you have believed in God, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims."﴾ ﴿So they said, "In God we have relied. Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people, ﴾ ﴿and save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people."﴾

*Meaning:* "Fa-ma amana li-Musa" means: none affirmed Moses as true. The verb *amana* (to believe) takes the preposition *bi-*, and it also takes *li-*, with the sense of *bi-* implied. The interpreters differed over what the pronoun in *qawmihi* ("his people") refers back to. One group said it refers to Moses, peace be upon him. Another group said it refers to Pharaoh.

Those who said it refers to Moses, peace be upon him, held that the verse describes the state of Moses at the beginning of his mission: that only young men and youths believed in him, most of them the children of fathers who lived under fear of Pharaoh and of the council of the Children of Israel. On this reading the pronoun in *al-mala'* ("the leaders") refers to *dhurriyyah* ("offspring"), and the *fa'* (so) here, on this interpretation, joins one clause to another without implying sequence.

Some who held that the pronoun refers to Moses, peace be upon him, said: the meaning of the verse is that Moses, peace be upon him, encountered a people who did not believe in him, and that their descendants believed only after their deaths, because of the long passage of time. This was said by Mujahid and al-A'mash. This view is not clear. If a people believed after the death of their fathers, there is no point in singling them out with the name *dhurriyyah*. Moreover, what is reported in the reports about the Children of Israel does not support this. The form of the statement *fa-ma amana* ("none believed") indicates that the number of believers was small, because it negates belief and then affirms it for some. Had the majority believed, it would have affirmed belief first and then negated it for a minority. On this reading, the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, about *dhurriyyah* is preferred: "It means the few." This does not mean that the word *dhurriyyah* itself means "few," as Makki and others thought.

A group said: they were called *dhurriyyah* because their mothers were from the Children of Israel while their fathers were from the Copts, so they were called "the offspring," just as the Persians of Yemen were called "the sons" (*abna'*). These were the Persians who moved with Wahraz at the instigation of Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan. The full account is in the biographies (*siyar*). Al-Suddi said: they were seventy households from the people of Pharaoh.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

What weakens the view that the pronoun refers to Moses, peace be upon him, is that it is well known from the reports about the Children of Israel that they were a people among whom prophets had come before. During the time of Pharaoh they suffered extreme humiliation, and they hoped that it would be lifted through a boy who would be born among them and would be a prophet. When Moses, peace be upon him, came to them, they crowded around him and followed him. It is never recorded that a group of the Children of Israel disbelieved in him. Then how can this verse imply that the minority among them were the ones who believed? According to this, what is preferred is that the pronoun refers to Pharaoh. This is also supported by what preceded: the dialogue of Moses, peace be upon him, with them, his responses to them, and his rebuke of them for their saying, "This is sorcery." God mentioned this about them, and then said: "None believed in Moses except some of the offspring of the people of Pharaoh," meaning those whose statements these were. It is reported on this matter that the wife of Pharaoh, his treasurer, the wife of his treasurer, and some youths from his people believed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father. The sorcerers are also counted among the people of Pharaoh. On this interpretation the story takes place after the manifestation of the sign and the challenge with the staff, and the *fa'* indicates sequence among the meanings it joins.

Because al-Farra' and others believed that the pronoun refers to Moses, peace be upon him, they became confused about the reference of the pronoun in *mala'ihim* ("their leaders"). Some of them said: the mention of Pharaoh, who is a king, implies the group and the soldiers, as you say, "The caliph came, and the king traveled," meaning his armies were with him. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "out of fear of the family of Pharaoh and their leaders," and this is of the type of: ﴿Ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 82).

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This comparison is not good, because dropping the *mudaf* (the governed noun) in ﴿Ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 82) is permissible because of what is understood by reason, namely that a town cannot ask. So the apparent meaning is evidence for what is omitted. Here, however, fear of Pharaoh is firmly established, and there is no need to supply anything with it. As for the claim that the plural pronoun in *wa-mala'ihim* requires this, fear is an attribute of actions and events that belong to a body. But because this usage is common, and for the sake of brevity, it is attributed to persons.

His statement ﴿that he would persecute them﴾ is a substitute for "Pharaoh," which is a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*). So *an* ("that") is in the genitive position. It may also be in the accusative position as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*). Al-Hasan and al-Jarrah read *an yuftinahum* with a *damma* on the *ya'*. Then He informed about Pharaoh with the attributes of exaltation in the land, excess in actions, killing, and claims, so that the excuse of those who feared would be clear.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And Moses said, "O my people"﴾ through ﴿the disbelieving people﴾. This begins the narration of the words of Moses, peace be upon him, to the group of the Children of Israel who believed among them, comforting them and calling them to rely upon God, in whose hand is victory. The question of *tawakkul* (reliance upon God) has many branches, and people have disputed it at length. What I say is: the reliance we have been commanded to practice is joined with a good means (*tasabbub*) in accordance with the Law. This is what is in his statement, peace be upon him: "Tie it and rely upon God." He made him a *mutawakkil* (one who relies) while tying it. The Prophet, peace be upon him, was the foremost of those who relied upon God, and he took means his whole life, and so did all the early generations (*salaf*). If a particular person deviates and abandons means entirely, that is a high rank, so long as he does not go to extremes with it, to the point of killing himself and destroying himself, such as one who enters a hidden cave and relies upon God there. This and similar things are disliked according to a group of scholars. What is reported of 'Amir ibn Qays confronting a lion and similar things is all weak. The sound part of such reports has supporting circumstances that make it acceptable. God said to all Muslims: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah 198). And to them He said: ﴿and upon God rely, if you are believers﴾ (al-Ma'idah 23). The statement of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in praise of the seventy thousand of his community: "and upon their Lord they rely" does not imply that they abandon means entirely. Nor is it recorded that 'Ukkasha abandoned means; rather, he would fight and take his arrows. By this I mean abandoning means in regard to food. As for abandoning means in regard to medicine, that is easy, and many people are disposed to it without intention or expectation of reward. How much more so for one who seeks reward.

He said to them: ﴿if you have believed﴾, while He knew their belief, in order to establish the proof, to awaken their souls, and to stir their pride, just as you say, "If you are a man, then fight," addressing a man whom you want to rouse to himself. His statement ﴿if you are Muslims﴾ means: people of obedience joined to the conditional faith. Thus the mention of Islam here adds a meaning. Then He mentioned that the Children of Israel responded with the intention of relying upon God and by voicing it. Then they prayed that He would not make them a trial for the wrongdoers. The meaning is: do not send upon us a calamity at their hands or by other means during our time living among them, so that they would be tested and would believe that our destruction is by Your intention, because of the corruption of our religion and the soundness of theirs, and that they are the people of truth. This was said by Mujahid and others.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This supplication, on this interpretation, includes averting two matters: first, killing and the calamity that the believers feared; second, the manifestation of polytheism, with its adherents believing that they are the people of truth. This involves corruption of the earth. A similar meaning is the statement of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "What a poor dead man Abu Umamah is for the Jews and polytheists, who say: 'If he had been a prophet, his companion would not have died.'" The wording admits other interpretations too, and a group has said that the meaning is: do not test them and afflict them by killing us, so that You would punish them for that in the Hereafter. But in this interpretation there is clear weakness.
