**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 10, verses 83–86:**

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿But none believed in Moses except some of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their leaders, that he would persecute them. Indeed, Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the extravagant.﴾ ﴿And Moses said, "O my people, if you have believed in God, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims."﴾ ﴿So they said, "In God we have relied. Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people, ﴾ ﴿and save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people."﴾

*Meaning:* "Fa-ma amana li-Musa" means: none affirmed Moses as true. The verb *amana* (to believe) takes the preposition *bi-*, and it also takes *li-*, with the sense of *bi-* implied. The interpreters differed over what the pronoun in *qawmihi* ("his people") refers back to. One group said it refers to Moses, peace be upon him. Another group said it refers to Pharaoh.

Those who said it refers to Moses, peace be upon him, held that the verse describes the state of Moses at the beginning of his mission: that only young men and youths believed in him, most of them the children of fathers who lived under fear of Pharaoh and of the council of the Children of Israel. On this reading the pronoun in *al-mala'* ("the leaders") refers to *dhurriyyah* ("offspring"), and the *fa'* (so) here, on this interpretation, joins one clause to another without implying sequence.

Some who held that the pronoun refers to Moses, peace be upon him, said: the meaning of the verse is that Moses, peace be upon him, encountered a people who did not believe in him, and that their descendants believed only after their deaths, because of the long passage of time. This was said by Mujahid and al-A'mash. This view is not clear. If a people believed after the death of their fathers, there is no point in singling them out with the name *dhurriyyah*. Moreover, what is reported in the reports about the Children of Israel does not support this. The form of the statement *fa-ma amana* ("none believed") indicates that the number of believers was small, because it negates belief and then affirms it for some. Had the majority believed, it would have affirmed belief first and then negated it for a minority. On this reading, the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, about *dhurriyyah* is preferred: "It means the few." This does not mean that the word *dhurriyyah* itself means "few," as Makki and others thought.

A group said: they were called *dhurriyyah* because their mothers were from the Children of Israel while their fathers were from the Copts, so they were called "the offspring," just as the Persians of Yemen were called "the sons" (*abna'*). These were the Persians who moved with Wahraz at the instigation of Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan. The full account is in the biographies (*siyar*). Al-Suddi said: they were seventy households from the people of Pharaoh.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

What weakens the view that the pronoun refers to Moses, peace be upon him, is that it is well known from the reports about the Children of Israel that they were a people among whom prophets had come before. During the time of Pharaoh they suffered extreme humiliation, and they hoped that it would be lifted through a boy who would be born among them and would be a prophet. When Moses, peace be upon him, came to them, they crowded around him and followed him. It is never recorded that a group of the Children of Israel disbelieved in him. Then how can this verse imply that the minority among them were the ones who believed? According to this, what is preferred is that the pronoun refers to Pharaoh. This is also supported by what preceded: the dialogue of Moses, peace be upon him, with them, his responses to them, and his rebuke of them for their saying, "This is sorcery." God mentioned this about them, and then said: "None believed in Moses except some of the offspring of the people of Pharaoh," meaning those whose statements these were. It is reported on this matter that the wife of Pharaoh, his treasurer, the wife of his treasurer, and some youths from his people believed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father. The sorcerers are also counted among the people of Pharaoh. Some of them said: the mention of Pharaoh, who is a king, implies the group and the soldiers, as you say, "The caliph came, and the king traveled," meaning his armies were with him. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "out of fear of the family of Pharaoh and their leaders," and this is of the type of: ﴿Ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 82).

[p. 516]

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 10, verses 87–89:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses, and make your houses a qiblah (a direction of prayer), and establish the prayer, and give good tidings to the believers."﴾ ﴿And Musa said: "Our Lord, You have given Fir'awn and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world. Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment."﴾ ﴿He said: "Your supplication has been answered, so remain upright, and do not follow the path of those who do not know."﴾

It is narrated that Fir'awn terrorised the Bani Isra'il and demolished the places they had taken for prayer and the like. [p. 517] So Allah revealed to Musa and Harun: "Choose and designate houses for the Bani Isra'il in Egypt." Mujahid said: "Misr in this verse means Alexandria, and Misr is from the stretch between the sea and Aswan, and Alexandria is part of the land of Egypt." Tabawwa'a (to settle, to take up residence), as we have said, means "to choose and take," and it is a word used for places and what resembles them. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Her affair is hers, until, when she has settled
for her cud a pasture, she settles her bed."

This verse is by al-Ra'i (the shepherd), and he was named after it. From it is also the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"They settle in positions for your fighting
like lions of a thicket whose night is roaring."

The people recited tabawwa'a with a hamzah, on the reckoning of (.....). Hafs, in the transmission of Hubayra, recited tabawwa'i (with the hamzah replaced by a yā'), and this is a facilitation which is not analogical. Had it followed analogy, it would have been between the hamzah and the alif.

His saying, ﴿qiblah﴾, means masajid (places of prostration/mosques). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i and others. They said: they feared, so they were commanded to pray in their houses. It was also said: some of them face others; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, but the first view is more correct. It was also said: the meaning is "directed towards the qiblah," said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. From this is a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The best of your houses is that in which the qiblah is faced."

His saying, ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, is addressed to the Bani Isra'il. This was before the descent of the Tawrah (Torah), because it was not revealed until after the crossing of the sea. His saying, ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, is a command to Musa, peace be upon him. Makki and al-Tabari said: it is a command to Muhammad (ﷺ). This is not firmly established.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Musa said﴾ (the verse). This is an outburst of anger from Musa, peace be upon him, against the Copts [p. 518] and an invocation against them. So before the invocation he set out the blessings of Allah upon them and their disbelief in them. "Atayta" means "You gave" and "You granted possession." The phrase ﴿Our Lord﴾ is repeated as an appeal, as the one calling upon Allah says. His saying ﴿li-yudillū (that they may lead astray)﴾ may be understood as the lām of purpose (lam al-kay) in its proper sense, meaning: You gave them wealth as a respite and gradual enticement (istidraj), so the giving was for the purpose of their going astray. It may also be understood as the lām of outcome and consequence (lam al-sayrurah wa al-'aqibah), as in His saying: ﴿So the family of Fir'awn picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. The meaning is: You gave them that, and their affair ended up in such-and-such. It is narrated from al-Hasan that he said: it is a supplication. It is also possible that the meaning is interrogative, i.e., "Our Lord, did You do that so that they might go astray?" In this there is an affirmation of the gravity of their offence.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu Ja'far, Mujahid, Abu Raja' and the people of Makkah recited ﴿li-yadillū﴾ with a fatha on the yā', meaning: that they might go astray within themselves. 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, Qatada, 'Isa, al-Hasan and al-A'raj (with a variant from him) recited ﴿li-yudillū﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā', meaning: that they might lead others astray. al-Sha'bi recited ﴿li-yidillū﴾ with a kasrah on the yā'.

Al-Sha'bi and others also recited ﴿u-ṭmus﴾ with a ḍammah on the mīm, and a group recited ﴿iṭmis﴾ with a kasrah on the mīm. Both are dialectal forms: it is said ṭamasa yaṭmisu and ṭamasa yaṭmusu. Abu Hatim said: the people's recitation is with a kasrah on the mīm, and the ḍammah is a well-known dialect. Its meaning is: to efface and to alter. It is from the effacement of a trace or an eye, and the obliteration of faces. From it is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"From every sweating, nodding-necked (she-camel), when she sweats,
her side is a faded, unknown sign."

[p. 519] It is narrated that when Musa, peace be upon him, made this supplication, their sugar (sukkar) and their provisions and their dinars and their grains of food turned back into stones. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Qatada and Ibn Zayd. Mujahid and others said: its meaning is: He destroyed them and ruined them. It is narrated that the obliteration (tamsah) was one of the nine signs of Musa, peace be upon him.

His saying ﴿and harden their hearts﴾ means: seal and lock their hearts upon disbelief. This was said by Mujahid and al-Dahhak. When 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, advised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to kill the prisoners of Badr, he likened him to Musa, peace be upon him, in his supplication against his people to whom he was sent in this verse, and to Nuh, peace be upon him, in his saying: ﴿Leave not upon the earth any of the disbelievers a dwelling-place﴾ [Nuh: 26].

His saying ﴿so that they will not believe﴾: the view of al-Akhfash and others is that the verb is in the accusative, coordinated with His saying "li-yudillū." It was also said that it is in the accusative as an answer to the imperative. al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said that it is in the jussive mood, as a supplication. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Let it not spread out between your eyes what has withdrawn,
and do not meet me except with your nose rubbed in the dust."

He made seeing the punishment the limit and end, because he knew from Allah, Exalted is He, that the believer, at the sight of the punishment, will not benefit from his faith at that time, nor will it remove him from his disbelief. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment."﴾ ﴿He said: "Your supplication has been answered, so remain upright, and do not follow the path of those who do not know."﴾

It is narrated that Fir'awn terrorised the Bani Isra'il and demolished the places they had taken for prayer and the like. [p. 517] So Allah revealed to Musa and Harun: "Choose and designate houses for the Bani Isra'il in Egypt." Mujahid said: "Misr in this verse means Alexandria, and Misr is from the stretch between the sea and Aswan, and Alexandria is part of the land of Egypt." Tabawwa'a (to settle, to take up residence), as we have said, means "to choose and take," and it is a word used for places and what resembles them. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Her affair is hers, until, when she has settled
for her cud a pasture, she settles her bed."

This verse is by al-Ra'i (the shepherd), and he was named after it. From it is also the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"They settle in positions for your fighting
like lions of a thicket whose night is roaring."

The people recited tabawwa'a with a hamzah, on the reckoning of (.....). Hafs, in the transmission of Hubayra, recited tabawwa'i (with the hamzah replaced by a yā'), and this is a facilitation which is not analogical. Had it followed analogy, it would have been between the hamzah and the alif.

His saying, ﴿qiblah﴾, means masajid (places of prostration/mosques). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i and others. They said: they feared, so they were commanded to pray in their houses. It was also said: some of them face others; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, but the first view is more correct. It was also said: the meaning is "directed towards the qiblah," said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. From this is a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The best of your houses is that in which the qiblah is faced."

His saying, ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, is addressed to the Bani Isra'il. This was before the descent of the Tawrah (Torah), because it was not revealed until after the crossing of the sea. The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak. What the wording of the Qur'an implies is that the Children of Israel had a large host in itself, yet small in comparison with the people of Pharaoh who pursued them.

A group said that the meaning of "bi-badanika" (بِبَدَنِكَ) is "with your armour" (bi-dir'ika). A group said its meaning is "with your person" (bi-shakhsika). A group recited "bi-nidā'ika" (بِنِدائِكَ), that is, with your statement: "I believe," to the end of the verse. It seems that "bi-nidā'ika" may have been written without an alif in some of the copies. The meaning of the verse is: We make you a sign together with your call, which does not benefit. A group recited "khalfaka" (خَلَفَكَ), meaning those who come after you. A group recited "khalfaka" (خَلْفَكَ), and the meaning is: God makes you a sign for Him among His servants.

Then the Mighty and Majestic made clear to His servants by His words: "And indeed many of the people are heedless of Our signs." This is a statement that implicitly contains a warning.

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement, and provided them with good things. And they did not differ until knowledge came to them. The meaning: We chose for the Children of Israel the best of choices, and settled them in the best of places. And ﴿mubawwa' sidq﴾ means a place in which the expectation of its intender, its dweller and its people is fulfilled. By this verse is meant their settlement in the lands of al-Sham (Greater Syria) and Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). This is said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. It was also said: the lands of Egypt and al-Sham; this is said by al-Dahhak. The first view is more sound, according to what has been preserved, that they would never return to Egypt. Moreover, the Qur'an says: ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 59], meaning what the Copts left of gardens, springs and other things. It is also possible that "awrathnaha" means the state of blessing, even if it was not in one region.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they did not differ until knowledge came to them﴾ admits of two meanings. One of them: they did not differ (p-526) concerning the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ until he came to them and his knowledge and his command became manifest, and then they differed.

This specification is what occurs in the books of the interpreters, and this interpretation needs a chain of transmission (sanad). The other interpretation which the wording admits is that the Children of Israel had no disagreement with Musa, peace be upon him, in the beginning of his state; then when knowledge and the commands came to them, and Pharaoh drowned, they differed.

So the meaning of the verse is a censure of that generation of the Children of Israel. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, made it obligatory after that that He would judge between them and decide, by punishing whom He punishes and having mercy on whom He has mercy.

Some of the interpreters said — and this was narrated from al-Hasan — that "in" is negative in meaning "ma", while the majority hold that "in" is conditional. The correct meaning of the verse is that it addresses the Prophet ﷺ, and what is intended by it is other than him, from every person who could doubt or oppose. Some people said: the speech is like your saying: "If you are my son, then be dutiful to me."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This example is not good. The closest example to this is His saying, the Exalted, to Isa: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two deities"?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. It is narrated that a man asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, about what occurs in the breast of doubt, and he said to him: No one escapes from that, not even the Prophet ﷺ, until this was revealed to him: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you.﴾

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Zahrawi mentioned that this statement was rejected as something Ibn 'Abbas could have said, and I say likewise, because (p-527) passing thoughts (al-khawatir) — none escapes from them — are other than the doubt about which one deliberates in order to be cured by asking. And ﴿those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾ are those among the Children of Israel who embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. And it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said when this verse was revealed: "I do not doubt, nor do I ask."

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, the people of Madinah, Abu 'Amr, 'Isa and 'Asim read "fa-sal" without hamza; while a great majority read it with hamza. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, affirmed the report with His saying: ﴿The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord﴾; the lam in "la-qad" is the lam of oath. "Al-mumtarin" means: the doubters who need, in their belief, to dispute about it. His saying: ﴿about what We have sent down to you﴾ intends: that the Children of Israel did not differ concerning his matter except after his coming; and this is the view of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) without exception.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is what most resembles that the removal of doubt about it might be hoped for from the side of the People of the Book. The wording admits that it may intend: by what We have sent down, the entire Shari'ah; but this is far in meaning, because that is not known, and doubt about it is removed only by the proofs of reason, not by hearing from the believers among the Children of Israel. And His saying: ﴿And do not be among those who denied﴾ the verse, is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ while the intent is others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

For this there is a benefit not present in addressing people with it directly, namely the intensity of warning: for if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is warned against the like of this, then others among the people are more deserving to beware and guard themselves.

﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ ﴿Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾ ﴿Why was there not a city that believed so its faith would benefit it—except the people of Jonah? (p-528) This was revealed as a repeated warning and an announcement of the bad state of those upon whom the decree has been fixed. The meaning is: Allah had decreed His wrath upon them from eternity and created them for His punishment, so they do not believe, even if every proof and every clarity should come to them, except at the time when faith will not benefit them, as Pharaoh and those like him among creation did, and that is the time of direct witnessing. Implicit in the wording is a warning against this state, and an urging of everyone to hasten to faith and to flee from the wrath of Allah.

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja' read "kalimatu" in the singular. Nafi' and the people of Medina read "kalimatu" in the plural. This variant has already been mentioned.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Why was there not a city that believed﴾ and so on: in the Codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud it reads "fahalla" (why not), and the meaning in both is the same. The original use of "lawla" (why not) in speech is tahdid (urging) or indicating the prevention of one matter due to the existence of another. This verse is far from both of these, but it belongs to the category of those that are for tahdid. The true nature of tahdid is that the one urging desires from the addressee that act which he urges him to do. "Lawla" may also come where the speaker does not intend that the addressee perform the act, in which case the meaning is reproach, as in the verse of Jarir:

"...................... ∗∗∗ lawla al-Kammiyya al-muqanna'a"

(Why not the armored, veiled horseman?)

He did not intend to urge them to slay the Kammiyy. Similarly, one says to a man who has fallen into a difficult matter: "Lawla taharrazta" (Why did you not take precaution?). This verse is of this kind.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What is understood from the meaning of the verse is the negation of the faith of the people of the cities, and the meaning of the verse is: "Why was there not one from the people of the city who believed (p-529) while they were at ease, the punishment not having yet overtaken them, so that faith would be beneficial in that state?" In meaning, it is connected, because its implied sense is: no one from the people of a city believed except the people of Jonah, peace be upon him. The accusative in His saying ﴿except the people of﴾ is the preferred reading, and for this reason Sibawayh placed it in the section of "what has nothing but the accusative." This is also the case with a disconnected exception. A comparable example is the verse of al-Nabigha:

"Except the stakes ..................."

This is the ruling of the wording of the verse. A group said: the nominative is also permissible, and this is a connected exception. Al-Mahdawi said: the nominative is in apposition to "qaryatun" (a city).

Ibn Jubayr said: the punishment covered them as a cloth covers a grave. Then Allah lifted the punishment from them. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 96–98:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ ﴿Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾ ﴿Why was there not a city that believed so its faith would benefit it—except the people of Jonah? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and gave them enjoyment for a time﴾

(p-528) This was revealed as a repeated warning and an announcement of the bad state of those upon whom the decree has been fixed. The meaning is: Allah had decreed His wrath upon them from eternity and created them for His punishment, so they do not believe, even if every proof and every clarity should come to them, except at the time when faith will not benefit them, as Pharaoh and those like him among creation did, and that is the time of direct witnessing. Implicit in the wording is a warning against this state, and an urging of everyone to hasten to faith and to flee from the wrath of Allah.

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja' read "kalimatu" in the singular. Nafi' and the people of Medina read "kalimatu" in the plural. This variant has already been mentioned.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Why was there not a city that believed﴾ and so on: in the Codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud it reads "fahalla" (why not), and the meaning in both is the same. The original use of "lawla" (why not) in speech is tahdid (urging) or indicating the prevention of one matter due to the existence of another. This verse is far from both of these, but it belongs to the category of those that are for tahdid. The true nature of tahdid is that the one urging desires from the addressee that act which he urges him to do. "Lawla" may also come where the speaker does not intend that the addressee perform the act, in which case the meaning is reproach, as in the verse of Jarir:

"...................... ∗∗∗ lawla al-Kammiyya al-muqanna'a"

(Why not the armored, veiled horseman?)

He did not intend to urge them to slay the Kammiyy. Similarly, one says to a man who has fallen into a difficult matter: "Lawla taharrazta" (Why did you not take precaution?). This verse is of this kind.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What is understood from the meaning of the verse is the negation of the faith of the people of the cities, and the meaning of the verse is: "Why was there not one from the people of the city who believed (p-529) while they were at ease, the punishment not having yet overtaken them, so that faith would be beneficial in that state?" Then He excepted the people of Jonah, peace be upon him. Grammatically it is an exception of disconnected type (istithna' munqati'), and this is how the grammarians all recorded it. In meaning, it is connected, because its implied sense is: no one from the people of a city believed except the people of Jonah, peace be upon him. The accusative in His saying ﴿except the people of﴾ is the preferred reading, and for this reason Sibawayh placed it in the section of "what has nothing but the accusative." This is also the case with a disconnected exception. A comparable example is the verse of al-Nabigha:

"Except the stakes ..................."

This is the ruling of the wording of the verse. A group said: the nominative is also permissible, and this is a connected exception. Al-Mahdawi said: the nominative is in apposition to "qaryatun" (a city).

It is narrated in the story of Jonah, peace be upon him, that when his people disbelieved, Allah revealed to him to warn them of punishment within three days. He did so, and they said: "He is a man who does not lie, so watch him. If he remains among you, there is no harm upon you; but if he departs from you, then it is certainly the descent of punishment." When night came, Jonah, peace be upon him, took provisions and left them. In the morning they did not find him, so they repented, called upon Allah, believed, wore sackcloth, and separated mothers from their children among the people and the animals. The punishment that came upon them, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, was over two-thirds of a mile. It is narrated from Ali that it was one mile. Ibn Jubayr said: the punishment covered them as a cloth covers a grave. Then Allah lifted the punishment from them. When the three days had passed and Jonah, peace be upon him, knew that the punishment had not descended, he said: "How shall I return, when they have found me to be a liar?" So he went away in anger, as Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned in this verse.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Tabari held that the people of Jonah, peace be upon him, were singled out among the nations in that repentance was accepted from them after witnessing the punishment. He reported this from a group of exegetes, but it is not so. The witnessing in which repentance no longer benefits is the punishment or death actually befalling a person, as in the story of Pharaoh. As for the people of Jonah, peace be upon him, they did not reach this limit.

Al-Hasan, Talha ibn Musarrif, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Ibn Wuththab, and al-A'mash read "Yunisa" with a kasra on the nun. In Arabic there are three dialects for this: the nun with damma, with fatha, and with kasra. The same applies to "Yusuf." His saying ﴿for a time﴾ means: until their appointed terms, which were decreed from eternity.

It is narrated that the people of Jonah, peace be upon him, were at Nineveh in the land of Mosul. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to 'Addas when he said to him that he was from the people of Nineveh: "From the town of the righteous man Jonah son of Matta?" This is the hadith in the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verse 99–101:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ ﴿And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah. And He places defilement upon those who do not reason.﴾ ﴿Say, "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth. But signs and warnings do not avail a people who will not believe."﴾

The meaning: All that has preceded occurred by the decree of Allah concerning them and His will regarding them. Had Allah willed, all of them would have been believers. So do not grieve, O Muhammad, over the disbelief of those who do not believe in you; call them, and do not be concerned about them, for the matter is decreed. Do you then wish to compel the people by bringing faith into their hearts and forcing them to it, while Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has willed otherwise?

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation makes the verse decisive (muhkamah) in this sense, i.e., call (to Islam) and fight whoever opposes you, and the faith of whoever believes is subject to the will (of Allah).

(p-531) A group said: The meaning is: "Would you compel the people by fighting until they enter into faith?" They claimed that this verse belongs to the early period of Islam and that it has been abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf). The verse, on both interpretations, refutes the Mu'tazilah. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿kulluhum jami'an﴾ ("all of them entirely") is emphasis (ta'kid), and it is from eloquent speech; "jami'an" is an emphatic circumstantial phrase (hal mu'akkidah). Similar to it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Do not take two gods﴾ [al-Nahl: 51].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾, the verse refers everything back to Allah, exalted is He, and that the power and capacity for the faith of whoever believes belongs to Allah, and that defilement is upon the disbelievers. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "wa-najʿalu al-rijsa" with the plural of majesty (nun of greatness), and the rest read, and Hafs from 'Asim, "wa-yajʿalu" with the ya'. Al-A'mash read "wa-yajʿalu Allahu al-rijsa." Al-rijs may mean punishment, like al-rijz, and may mean filth and impurity, like al-riks; Abu 'Ali mentioned this here and others. In this verse it means punishment. "Those who do not reason" refers to the signs of Allah and the proofs of the Law. The meaning of "permission" (idhn) in this verse is will and decree for that; it is thus knowledge and enablement (tamkin).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth"﴾ This verse is a command to the disbelievers to reflect and contemplate the created things that indicate the Maker and other signs of the heavens, their spheres, stars and clouds and the like, and the earth, its plants, minerals and other things. The meaning: Reflect upon these as is obligatory, for it will alert you to knowledge of Allah and belief in His oneness. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and the common readers of Basra read "qul unzuru" with a kasra on the lam, while Nafi' and the people of Madinah read "qul unzuru" with a damma on the lam. Then, at the end of the verse, He informs that looking at the signs and hearing from the warnings (nudhur), who are the prophets, avails only by the will of Allah, and that this is not beneficial for a people for whom Allah has decreed that they will not believe. This is on the basis that "ma" is negative. It is also permissible to take it as an interrogative in the form of affirmation which implies the negation of the occurrence of benefit. In the verse, according to this, there is a rebuke for the polytheists present with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His saying: ﴿the signs and the warnings﴾ restricts the paths by which Allah makes Himself known to His servants. It is possible that "wa-ma" in His saying ﴿wa-ma tughni﴾ is an object of ﴿unzuru﴾, coordinated with His saying ﴿madha﴾, meaning: Consider the extent of the benefit that the signs and warnings bring to the disbelievers if they accept them, like the act of the people of Yunus, peace be upon him, for he removes punishment in this world and the Hereafter and saves from (p-532) destructions. The verse, on this view, is an exhortation to faith.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The figurative usage of the expression, on this interpretation, lies only in His saying: (they do not believe).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 102–104:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Are they waiting for anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say: "Wait, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ ﴿Then We save Our messengers and those who believe. Thus it is incumbent upon Us: We shall save the believers.﴾ ﴿Say: "O mankind, if you are in doubt about my religion, then I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah; rather I worship Allah, who causes you to die. And I have been commanded to be among the believers."﴾

This is a warning and an exhortation to faith, meaning: if they persist in disbelief, punishment will befall them, and if they believe, they will be saved. This is the way of Allah with the nations that passed before. So do these people expect anything other than that? The interrogative here carries the sense of rebuke.

In His words, ﴿Say: "Wait"﴾, there is a kind of temporary truce (muhadana), and it is among the things abrogated (mansukh) by fighting (qital).

As for His words, ﴿Then We save Our messengers﴾ and the verse that follows: since the time of punishment is not limited and the Prophet and the believers were among the disbelievers, it is explicitly stated that the custom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has been established in saving His messengers and their followers. Thus the warning, in this light, is even stronger. All of them read "nunajji" with a doubled jim, except al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim, who read "nunji" with a sukun on the nun and a single jim. In some transmissions from 'Asim in Surat al-Anbiya', he read "nujji" with a damma on the nun, dropping the second letter and doubling the jim, as if the nun had been assimilated into it; this is a reading for which there is no basis, as mentioned by al-Zajjaj. Abu Hatim reported something similar from al-A'mash. The orthography of the Mushaf for this word is "nunj" with an unpointed jim and without a ya', and likewise al-Kisa'i read in Surat Maryam: "thumma nunji alladhina ittaqaw" with a sukun on the nun and a single jim, while the rest read with a fatha on the nun and a doubled jim. The kaf in His words "thus" (kadhalika) may be in the nominative position, and it may be in the accusative position as an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar).

As for His words, ﴿Say: "O mankind"﴾ and the verse that follows: it is a general address to all mankind until the Day of Resurrection, and it includes everyone who is characterized by doubt concerning the religion of Islam. The meaning of this verse is consistent with certain omitted elements indicated by this brief apparent wording. The meaning is: if you are in doubt about my religion, then you do not worship Allah; likewise, He is not one who should be doubted, and what is doubted and rejected is your religion. As for "I do not worship anyone other than Him," the eloquence and conciseness of the speech required the omission of all of this. Then he named the one he worships and specified among His attributes ﴿who causes you to die﴾, because of what this carries of reminder of death, of striking souls with it, of the return to Allah after it, and of the rejection of the idols which they believed to be harmful and beneficial.

Then he named the one he worships and specified among His attributes ﴿who causes you to die﴾, because of what this carries of reminder of death, of striking souls with it, of the return to Allah after it, and of the rejection of the idols which they believed to be harmful and beneficial.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 105–107:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And set your face toward the religion, as a upright monotheist (ḥanīfan), and do not be among the polytheists.﴾ ﴿And do not call upon, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you nor harm you. If you do, then you would indeed be among the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him. And if He intends for you good, there is none to repel His bounty. He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants. And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾

The meaning: It was said to me: "Be among the believers, and set your face toward the religion." Then the expression came in this order. The word "face" (wajh) in this verse means direction and purpose, that is: make your path and your reliance be upon the religion and the Law. "Ḥanīfan" (upright) means "upright," according to the view of one who said: al-ḥanaf is uprightness, and who made the naming of a crooked foot as aḥnaf (having a bent foot) a case of optimism (tafā'ul). Whoever said: "al-ḥanaf is inclination" made "ḥanīfan" here mean: inclining away from the condition and path of the disbelievers. "Ḥanīfan" is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl). The saying ﴿and do not call upon﴾ means: it was said to me: "and do not call upon," so it is conjoined to "aqim" (set). This command and address is to the Prophet (ﷺ); if this is the case for him, then it is more fitting that others guard against it. "That which neither benefits nor harms" refers to the idols and images. The wrongdoer (ẓālim) is one who places a thing in other than its place.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾ and the rest of the verse, the aim of this verse is that power and strength belong to Allah. He makes this clear to people through what they perceive in themselves. Ḍurr (harm) is a comprehensive term for everything a person dislikes, whether it be in his wealth or in his body. This verse makes manifest the corruption of the condition of the idols, for every discerning person, with the least discernment, knows with certainty that they cannot remove harm nor bring about benefit.

As for his saying: ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾, it is a word of complete generality. The Prophet (ﷺ) specified understanding of the religion by mention in his saying: "Whoever Allah intends good for, He grants him understanding in the religion," and this is in the manner of honoring understanding (al-fiqh). His saying the Exalted: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is a expression of hope, extension, and a general promise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 10, verses 108–109:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: O mankind, the truth has come to you from your Lord. Whoever is guided, it is only for his own soul that he is guided; and whoever goes astray, it is only against it that he goes astray. And I am not over you a guardian.﴾ ﴿And follow what is revealed to you, and be patient until Allah judges, and He is the best of judges.﴾

This is an address to all the disbelievers, continuing throughout time. "The truth" is the Qur'an and the sacred law (shar') that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. ﴿Whoever is guided﴾, that is, follows the truth and submits to it, then he strives only for his own soul, because he thereby brings upon it the mercy of Allah and averts His punishment. ﴿And whoever goes astray﴾, that is, deviates from the path of truth and does not look with the eye of reality, and disbelieves in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, then it is the opposite of that. His saying: ﴿And I am not over you a guardian﴾, that is: (p-535) I am not one who will compel you to faith, necessarily; I am only a conveyer of the message. And this verse is abrogated (mansukha) by the fighting (qital).

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you﴾, the verse's meaning is: follow what your sacred law has laid down for you, and what Allah has informed you of concerning His support for you. And be patient over the hardship of the message and the harm that reaches you for the sake of Allah. His saying: ﴿until Allah judges﴾ is a promise to the Prophet (ﷺ) that He will make them prevail, as it happened, as the strength of the wording requires. This patience is abrogated by fighting. This surah is Meccan, and the mention of this has already preceded at its beginning.

End of the tafsir of Surah Yunus, with the help and success of Allah, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
